chapters.name: The Lost Ribbon
chapters.content:
The thaw came late that year, as if the winter were loath to give Blackwood Hall up. For weeks the yard stayed a sheet of old bone, and the north drawing room window stayed fogged with her breath, and Rosalind stood at the glass and watched the same slow turning circle she had watched all winter—only now the circle was different, because now he knew she was there, and because now, when he looked up, he looked at her.

That was the change the colic night had made. Before, his eyes had slid past the window as if it were empty glass. Now, crossing the yard with a bucket of steaming water, or leading Willow to her noon walk, he would glance up—quick, sidelong, gone again—and Rosalind, hidden in the curtain's shadow, would feel her heart knock against her ribs in that particular, terrible, wonderful way. She had read about such hearts in the novels she was not supposed to read and had believed them exaggeration. They were not.

They did not speak. That was the strange miracle of those weeks—that two people could carry on a conversation without a single word, across a frozen yard, through a pane of glass. He would come out of the stable block at first light and stand a moment in the doorway, stamping his boots, and look up at the north window before beginning his work. That was his good morning. She would be there—she was always there now, rising in the dark, to Elsie's quiet bewilderment—and she would lift her hand, just a little, just inside the curtain, so that only he could see. And he would lower his head and go to the pump, and she would watch the set of his shoulders ease, as if something in him had been waiting for that small lifted hand and had now been told: all is well.

She catalogued his mornings the way she had once catalogued the cliff birds. He fed the horses before he fed himself. He limped less now that the frost had broken. He had mended the patch at his left elbow with a neatness that suggested patience, and the stitching was a different color from the coat, and Rosalind, who had never noticed a servant's mending in her life, noticed it and treasured it. He spoke to the grey stallion in that low current of sound she could almost feel through the pane, and the stallion lowered its head to him like a great dog, and she thought: he is kind. That is all. He is simply kind. And her world had taught her that kindness was a currency spent on the valuable and withheld from the worthless, and here was a boy spending it freely on a cast-off mare and a stallion nobody else would touch—and on a lady at a window who had done nothing to earn it except stand there, seen.

One morning he found a scrap of dove-grey ribbon in the yard, dropped by a kitchen girl the day before, and he picked it up, turned it in his scarred fingers, and looked up at the window. Rosalind's breath caught. For a moment she thought he meant to keep it, and the thought of it—a piece of ribbon hidden in his loft above the horses—sent a heat through her she had no name for. But he only tucked it into his coat pocket, and at noon he returned it to the girl who had lost it, and she bobbed a curtsy, and he walked on as if it had cost him nothing.

It cost him nothing, of course. It was a ribbon. And yet Rosalind felt something precise as a needle settle in her chest: she wanted to be the girl who dropped a ribbon in his yard and had it returned to her by those careful, scarred hands. She wanted to give him something, and to have him keep it.

She thought about it for a week. A ribbon, deliberately dropped. It would be an accident, of course—an accident she had arranged with the same silent cunning with which she had arranged her days around the window. She would pass the stable block on some invented errand, her blue ribbon trailing, and she would let it fall where he would find it, and he would pick it up and know, and the returning of it would be a word spoken, a line crossed.

The ribbon she chose was blue. It was the color of the new gown being made for the Derwents' ball, the blue of a summer sky Blackwood Hall rarely saw. It had come off a bonnet her mother had worn in the portrait that hung in her room—painted while her mother was still young and smiling, before the wasting illness—and Rosalind told herself she chose it because it was the prettiest she owned, and not because it felt like taking her mother with her into whatever was about to begin. She tied it loosely among the curls at her nape one grey afternoon in late March, and looked at herself in the glass, and her own eyes looked back at her, bright and afraid.

She rehearsed the walk: down the back stairs, along the passage to the kitchen wing, out through the side door onto the yard. She had told Elsie she was going to the stillroom for a headache powder, which was a lie, and Elsie had looked at her in that quiet, knowing way of hers and said nothing, and Rosalind felt the first small prickle of unease. Elsie saw more than she let on.

The yard was grey and empty when she came out. The thaw had turned the frozen sheet to mud, and her slippers sank at the edges. She made herself breathe, and walked unhurried along the edge of the yard, past the pump, past the woodpile, toward the stable block, where the grey stallion's head hung over the half-door, watching her with dark, patient eyes. Drawing level with the stable door, she reached up as if to adjust her hair, and the blue ribbon slipped free and fell into the mud at her feet, a small bright wound in all that grey.

She did not look at it. She walked around the corner of the stable block, out of sight, and leaned against the cold stone wall with her heart hammering. She had given him her mother's ribbon, and she did not know if he would understand, or give it to the kitchen girls as he had given them the grey scrap, or keep it, or throw it away. She had no right to ask anything of him. She had only the wanting, and the terrible vulnerability of a gift that could not be explained away.

She heard footsteps. Slow, deliberate. Then he was there, around the corner, close enough that she could smell the hay and horses on his coat, holding the ribbon. It was clean—he must have wiped the mud from it with his shirt hem—and his hands, those scarred, careful hands she had watched through glass all winter, were trembling.

"My lady," he said, his voice scraped bare the way she remembered it from the frozen yard at dawn. "You dropped this."

She looked at the ribbon in his hands, then at his face. He was not looking at her; he was looking at the ribbon, as if it were a live thing that might startle. "I did," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she wanted. "Thank you."

He held it out. His hand shook, the tremor running through his fingers. And Rosalind, instead of taking it, put her hand beneath his, so that his hand lay in her palm and the ribbon lay between them, and for one long moment neither of them moved.

Then he looked up. Their eyes met, and the air between them went thick and strange, and Rosalind felt the whole of her carefully arranged life tilt. She had wanted him to see her. She had not understood that being seen could feel like this—like standing at the edge of a cliff, like falling.

"Callum," she said. Just his name. It had been living in her mouth since the dawn she had first spoken it, and now she spoke it again, and his face did the thing she had seen once before—the wariness falling away, the loosening—and he smiled, small and brief and devastating, and said, "Aye, my lady."

The moment held. Then a door banged somewhere in the kitchen wing, and the spell broke, and Callum stepped back a full pace and pressed the ribbon into her palm with a gentleness that felt like an apology.

"You should go in," he said, exactly as he had at dawn, and Rosalind knew he was saying something else underneath it: that she was the Earl's daughter and he was the stable hand, and there were lines in that house that a man crossed at his peril, and he would not ask her to cross them.

She closed her fingers around the ribbon. It was warm from his hand. "Will you keep it?" she asked, the words out before she could stop them, and she saw the shock of them land on him. "Not the ribbon," she said quickly, heat flooding her face. "The knowing of it. That I dropped it for you. That it was not an accident."

He stared at her. The silence stretched, and she felt herself begin to shake, and then he said, very low, "I know it wasn't." And before she could speak: "I'll keep the knowing."

She had not known a person could say a thing like that and mean it. She nodded, unable to speak, and turned, and walked back across the muddy yard with the blue ribbon crushed in her fist, and she felt his eyes on her back the whole way, and she did not look back.

That night she sat on the edge of her mother's bed and smoothed the ribbon out across her knee. It was damp and faintly mud-stained, and she did not clean it. She folded it instead into the pages of her private chronicle, the little book in which she had kept her silent record of him, and pressed the pages flat, and understood, with the cold clarity that had always been the only honest thing in her life, that the watching had become something else entirely.

She could have named it obsession. In the dark of her room she did name it, silently: she was obsessed with him. Every hour of her day bent toward the next glimpse of him. She woke early to see him at the pump. She found excuses to cross the yard—stillroom errands, walks to the garden, a sudden interest in the condition of the stables that made even her father raise an eyebrow. They had not spoken since the day of the ribbon—had not dared—but the ribbon lay in her chronicle, and the knowing lay in him, and the silence between them had become a thing with a shape and a weight.

Elsie noticed. Of course Elsie noticed. She had been noticing for weeks, in that quiet way of hers: the ruined dress at dawn, the rising before light, the stillroom errand that had produced no powder and a mud-splashed hem, the hours at the north window, the way her mistress's hands went still over her embroidery and stayed still. She said nothing; she unbuttoned Rosalind's pearls and hung her dresses and curtsied and withdrew, her careful mouth closed, her clever eyes taking everything in. But one evening, standing behind Rosalind at the mirror as she worked the pins from her hair, Elsie met her mistress's eyes in the glass and said, very softly, "You've been going to the window a great deal, my lady."

Rosalind's heart stopped, then ran on too fast. "The light is better there," she said, which was a lie, and she saw Elsie's reflection take it in and set it aside with the same gentle patience she used on a snarl in a ribbon.

"Mm," Elsie said, and her fingers moved on, deft and silent, and Rosalind understood that Elsie had seen more than she had been told. The prickle of unease at the stillroom door returned, colder now, and she pushed it down, because she could not afford to think about what Elsie might do with what she had seen, or what her father might do if the seeing ever reached him. She could only afford the next morning, and the next glimpse of him at the pump, and the small lifted hand inside the curtain that was their good morning now, their blue ribbon made of light.

Weeks passed. The spring came on slowly, greening the edges of the moors. And Rosalind, standing at the north window with the blue ribbon folded against her palm beneath her sleeve—she had begun to carry it with her, always, a secret pressed to her skin—watched Callum lead Willow across the yard at her unhurried pace, one hand on her neck, his mouth moving in that low current of sound, and she thought: this is what I want. Not the ball at Merriwether House, not the blue gown, not the provincial daughters her father had warned her not to outshine. This. A boy and a horse and a private language, and the terrible knowledge that he was keeping her, as she was keeping him, in the warm dark behind his ribs.

She did not know what would come of it. She only knew that the watching had become a wanting, the wanting a need, the need the shape of her days—and that the ribbon, folded in her chronicle, hidden against her palm, was no longer her mother's. It was his. It had been his from the moment his trembling hands had held it out to her and he had said, I'll keep the knowing.

It was the most precious thing she owned. It was the only thing she owned. And she carried it with her, everywhere, like a pulse.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth
set.description: Seventeen-year-old only daughter of the Earl of Ashworth. Lives at Blackwood Hall in her late mother's cold rooms; sleeps in her mother's bed under faded damask, her mother's portrait on the wall. Restless, intelligent, secretly reads novels. Since the colic night she has been seen and warmed, and over the weeks since she has descended into a full, unnameable obsession with Callum: she rises before light to catch him at the pump, finds invented errands to cross the yard, watches from the north drawing room window, and exchanges a silent private language with him (her small lifted hand inside the curtain is their good morning). In late March she deliberately dropped her mother's blue bonnet ribbon near the stables; he returned it with trembling hands; she confessed it was no accident and he said he would 'keep the knowing.' She folded the ribbon into the pages of her private chronicle of him and now carries it with her everywhere, pressed to her skin, a talisman. She has not cleaned the mud from it. She dreads the Derwents' autumn ball at Merriwether House and the blue gown being made by Mrs. Haversham. Elsie has begun to notice her distraction; Rosalind lied that the window had better light. Emotional condition: transformed, hungry, afraid, newly alive; the watching has become a wanting, the wanting a need; she knows the connection is no longer mere observation. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: to see him, to be seen by him; no language yet for what she wants beyond the next glimpse.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: The Earl of Ashworth, a cold, prideful man carved from grey stone who treats Rosalind as property and keeps his own portrait in his study. Unaware that his daughter crossed the yard at dawn, unaware of the stable hand's name or any connection between them, unaware his daughter has begun secretly dropping ribbons and carrying them against her skin. Once dismissed the foundling stable boy with a wave without looking up from his ledger. Ordered a new blue gown for the Derwents' autumn ball at Merriwether House and warned Rosalind not to outshine provincial daughters; he raised an eyebrow at her sudden interest in the stables but did not pursue it. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: preserve the Ashworth name and bloodline; marry Rosalind off advantageously.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's lady's maid, a quiet girl from the village with clever hands and a careful mouth. Loyal and discreet, but observant: she found the dress wet to the knee and muddied at dawn after the colic night and dried it in silence, and in the weeks since she has been noticing more — her mistress rising before light, hours at the north window, stillroom errands that produced no powder and mud-splashed hems, hands going still over embroidery. One evening at the mirror she gently asked why Rosalind had been going to the window so much; Rosalind lied about the light, and Elsie accepted it with quiet patience, but she has not been fooled. She has not yet connected the distraction to the stable hand Callum by name, nor understood its depth, and she has not yet been told anything. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: serve her mistress; she watches and keeps her own counsel.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old stable hand at Blackwood Hall, lean and dark with slate-dark hair and near-black guarded eyes; limps slightly on cold mornings; found half-starved on the moor road eleven years ago by Ned Tarrant; gave himself his name on the long walk; sleeps in a loft above the horses; mends his own coat. Gift with horses that cannot be taught or bought; walks the lame chestnut mare Willow three times daily; the grey stallion no one else approaches lowers its head to him. Since the colic night and the dawn when the lady from the window came down and spoke to him, something has been loosening in him. Over the following weeks they exchanged a silent language: he looks up at the north window before beginning work; her small lifted hand inside the curtain is his good morning. He picked up a kitchen girl's dropped grey ribbon and returned it — and then, one grey afternoon in late March, the lady dropped a blue ribbon near the stable door and he returned it to her with trembling hands, telling her he knew it was not an accident; when she asked him to keep the knowing, he said, low, 'I'll keep the knowing.' He keeps his distance by rank — he sent her back inside before the kitchen woke — but the guarded warmth he keeps for horses has fully turned on her; he keeps her, as she keeps him, in the warm dark behind his ribs. Goal: survival; he never dared want more, but he wants this now and is afraid of the wanting. Location: Blackwood Hall stables.

In late March, Rosalind deliberately dropped her mother's blue bonnet ribbon near the stable block. Callum returned it to her with trembling hands; she confessed it was not an accident and asked him to keep the knowing of it, and he said 'I'll keep the knowing.' The ribbon became the talisman of their unspoken bond: she folded it into her private chronicle and carries it with her everywhere, and their stolen glances across the courtyard became a private language. (The ribbon must later pass into Callum's keeping so it can be returned to her after his death.)

One evening at the mirror Elsie gently remarked that Rosalind had been going to the north window a great deal; Rosalind lied that the light was better there. Elsie accepted it in silence but was not fooled — she has begun quietly watching her mistress's distraction without yet connecting it to Callum by name. This positions Elsie as the one who will later be trusted with the secret, and eventually betrayed under threat of the whip.

The blue ribbon (her mother's bonnet ribbon, now Rosalind's talisman) must pass into Callum's keeping in a later chapter — he must come to possess it (e.g., she gives it to him, or he takes it from her hair in the hayloft), so that after his death it can be returned to her in the oilskin package in Ch. 19 'The Ribbon's Return.'

chapters.name: The Hayloft
chapters.content:
It began, as so many of the worst and best things did, with her father's voice.

He had kept her standing in his study for a full quarter of an hour, which was his way of reminding her that she was a petitioner in her own house. The grey afternoon light fell through the tall windows, and the Earl of Ashworth sat behind his ledger like a man carved from the same stone as the house, and he did not ask her to sit.

"I am told," he said, without looking up, "that Mrs. Haversham has finished the bodice of the blue gown."

"Yes, Papa."

"And that it fits you." He turned a page. "I am also told," he said, in the same flat tone, "that you have been seen in the stable yard. Often. That you have taken to crossing it at hours when a lady has no business out of doors."

Rosalind's blood went cold, but she kept her face still. "I walk in the mornings," she said. "For the air."

"For the air," her father repeated, and finally looked up, and his eyes were the grey of the winter sea. "The servants talk, Rosalind. They talk about what the Earl's daughter does, and where she does it, and at what hour. The Derwents' ball is in five months. You will be seen there by every family of consequence in the county, and you will be judged." He closed the ledger with a soft, final sound. "I will not have my daughter known as the girl who haunts the stables."

Her throat closed. She thought of the north window, of the small lifted hand, of a boy and a lame mare crossing a muddy yard—and the thought of those things being dragged into this cold room and held up to the light made her want to be sick. "I have done nothing," she said.

"You have been seen doing nothing," he said, "and that is enough. See that you are not seen doing it again. You may go."

He had already turned back to his ledger. She had been dismissed as one dismisses a servant. She curtsied—she always curtsied; it was the only language he understood—and walked out of the study on legs that did not tremble until the door was shut behind her.

And then she fled.

She did not go to her room. She went down the back stairs and out through the side door into the yard, her indoor slippers finding the mud, not caring, her breath coming short and hot. The spring dusk was gathering, the sky a bruised grey, and the yard was empty, and she walked blindly along its edge and turned in at the stable door without deciding to, because the smell of hay and horses was the only warm thing left in the world, and because somewhere in the warm dark ahead of her there was a lantern.

She followed it up. The ladder to the hayloft was steep and she climbed it in her fine skirts, mud on her hem, and pushed up the trap and rose into a golden cave of straw.

He was there. Of course he was there—the lantern was his. He sat cross-legged on a spread of sacking in the middle of the hay, a bridle across his knee, a needle and waxed thread in his hands, and the lamplight fell over him like a held breath. He looked up at the sound of her, and his face did something complicated—shock, then wariness, then, underneath it, a loosening she had learned to read from a hundred yards away.

"My lady," he said, and started to rise.

"Don't." Her voice came out too high. "Please—don't. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to—I saw the light—"

He settled back, slowly, and set the bridle down, and waited. And Rosalind stood in the mouth of the trap with the cold draft at her back and the warm gold air against her face, and understood that she had nowhere left to run to and no reason to run at all.

"I had to get out," she said. "Of the house. He—" She stopped and pressed her hand to her mouth, horrified to find she was shaking.

Callum did not move. He watched her with those dark, guarded eyes, and then he said, very gently, "Sit down, my lady, before you fall down."

She sat. The hay was warm and gave under her, and the smell of it rose up around her—dry grass, dust, leather, horses—and she realized she could not remember the last time she had sat on anything that was not upholstered or polished or her own. She laughed, a small broken sound, and pressed her hand over her mouth again.

He waited. He did not ask. That was the first thing she noticed, that he did not ask.

Presently the shaking stopped, and the hayloft settled around them like a room that had been waiting all her life to be entered. Below, she could hear the horses shifting in their stalls, the grey stallion's deep, contented breath, and somewhere Willow whickered softly in her sleep. The lantern swung a little on its hook, pushing the shadows back and forth across his face.

"He said the servants talk," Rosalind said at last. "He said I have been seen in the yard, and that I am to be judged at the Derwents' ball, and that I will not be known as the girl who haunts the stables." She heard how the sentence came out—her father's coldness wrapped around her own voice—and hated it. "As if I were a horse he was breaking for sale."

Callum picked up the bridle again and ran the waxed thread through his fingers, and she watched his hands do their quiet work. "The yard has eyes," he said. "I know. I've been careful." He looked up at her, briefly. "But you can't be seen coming here, my lady. You know that."

"I know." The words felt like stepping off a ledge. "And I came anyway."

Something moved in his face at that—the loosening again, the thing that happened when she said his name at dawn or dropped a ribbon in his yard. He looked down at the bridle and worked his needle through the leather, and she watched the set of his shoulders ease, the way they eased when the grey stallion lowered its head to him.

"Whose bridle is that?" she asked, because she could not bear the silence to harden between them, and because she genuinely wanted to know.

"The stallion's." He turned it so she could see the cheekpiece, where the leather was rubbed thin and a line of new stitching ran clean and even along the old split. "He throws his head when he's led. Snaps the keepers." A pause. "A bridle mended well outlasts one bought new. My father—" He stopped, and a strange look crossed his face, and he said, "I mean, the man who taught me. Ned Tarrant. He says a thing you've fixed with your own hands is yours in a way a new thing never is."

"Did he teach you to read too?" she asked, before she could stop herself, and immediately flushed. "I'm sorry. I only wondered—the stitching, you do it so—" She was making it worse. "How do you know how to do all of this?"

He was quiet a moment, threading the needle again. "I taught myself to read," he said. "There was an almanac Ned threw out, the pages loose, and I kept them. I wanted to know what the stars were called." He gestured upward, past the beams and the roof to the sky she could not see. "You watch the sky long enough and you start wanting names for things. The Pleiades. Orion. The Plough. I know the sea's weather from the cliff birds, too—when the gulls come inland, a storm's building. Ned says I read the world the way other men read a book."

Rosalind stared at him. He had grown up in this yard with nothing, and he had taught himself the names of the stars. She had grown up with a library she had never once been encouraged to enter, and she had never thought to wonder what anything was called—only to long for things she had no names for. The whole arrangement of the world suddenly seemed to her an outrageous fraud.

"Say one," she said. "Say what you see."

He looked up at her, and in the lantern light his eyes were almost black, and he said, low, "Orion. He's out over the sea tonight. My lady—" He stopped, and set the bridle down, and she saw his hands, those scarred careful hands, were not quite steady. "Rosalind."

The sound of her name in his mouth went through her like warm water. She had heard it a thousand times, from her father's stone voice and Elsie's gentle one and a hundred servants' curtsying murmurs, and she had never once heard it the way he said it—like a thing he had been holding behind his teeth and had finally, carefully set down.

"Yes," she said. "Here. Like that. Not my lady. Here, I am Rosalind."

He nodded slowly, and the air between them seemed to change, to grow a shape and a weight. "Here," he repeated, and it was a vow.

Below them the grey stallion stamped once and settled. The lantern flame leaned and righted itself. And Rosalind, sitting in the warm straw with mud drying on her hem and her name still hanging in the air between them, found herself telling him things she had never told anyone. Not the great secret—not yet—but the true ones: that she read novels hidden in her room and burned them when she finished because she had nowhere to keep them; that she had catalogued the cliff birds the way he catalogued the stars, wanting names, wanting to be sure the world was real; that the blue gown was being made to show her off like a horse at a fair, and that her mother had worn a gown like it in the portrait, painted before the wasting illness, smiling, and that Rosalind looked at it every night and wondered which of them the smile was for.

He listened. He did not interrupt, and he did not look away, and when she ran out of words he was quiet so long she thought she had said too much, and then he said, "My lady—Rosalind." He said the name like he was testing its weight and finding it good. "You asked how I know how to do all of this. It's because I watch. I watch everything. I've watched you all winter from the yard—the grey at the window, the hand that lifts in the morning. I know the hours you keep and the way you cross a yard like you expect it to bite you. I know you carry something in your sleeve, because you touch it when you think no one sees." He looked at her, and there was no guile in his face, only that terrible observant gentleness. "I watch, and I keep what I see."

The blood rushed to her face, and her hand flew to her sleeve, and the small folded weight of the ribbon was there against her wrist, where it had been every hour since the grey afternoon he had returned it to her.

"You see this," she whispered, and drew it out—a thread of blue in the lamplight, faded at the edges, mud-stained and never cleaned. His mother's ribbon, her mother's ribbon, hers. "You gave it back to me, and I told you to keep the knowing, and I—" She held it out, a small bright wound in all that gold. "I keep it with me. Always. I press it against my skin and I think—" She could not finish. She held it out to him instead, an offering she had not known she was carrying toward this moment.

His hand rose. His fingers brushed the silk, and hers, and the touch was like the ribbon had been—a line crossed, a word spoken. For one long moment she thought she would let it go, and he would keep it, and everything would change.

Then the stallion below threw his head against the stall and the chain rattled, loud as a slap, and they both started, and the spell broke, and Rosalind closed her fingers around the ribbon and drew it back to her chest, breathing hard.

"I can't," she said, not knowing if she meant it. "Not yet. It's the only thing—" The only thing that is mine, she almost said, and did not.

Callum looked at her hand, closed over the blue silk, and nodded slowly. "Keep it," he said. "Keep it till you're ready. I'll keep the knowing. I've told you I would." And he smiled then, small and brief and devastating, the way he had smiled at her in the frozen yard at dawn. "And you can keep this place. Whenever you need to get out—the lantern will be lit. I mend a lot of bridles."

She laughed, and the laugh came out clean and true, and she realized she could not remember the last time she had laughed like that in her father's house. She sat a while longer in the warm gold dark, and he talked about Willow's walking, and the stallion's moods, and the way the moor road looked from the top of the yard at night, and she listened, and the word lord came into her head and stood there, and she thought: he is smarter and kinder than any lord I have ever known, and he sees me, and none of them ever have, and I do not know what to do with that.

At last the wind came up around the eaves, and the cold found its way in, and she knew she had to go before the house woke to find her gone. She rose, and he rose with her, and at the mouth of the trap he steadied her elbow with one hand—a touch so light it might have been an accident, except that it was not, and they both knew it.

"Tomorrow," she said. It was not a question.

"Whenever the lantern's lit," he said. "I'll keep it burning."

She climbed down the ladder into the dark, and the warm smell of him and the hay and the horses fell away behind her, and she crossed the yard with mud on her hem and the ribbon pressed against her wrist, and went in by the side door and up the back stairs, and lay in her mother's bed with her eyes open in the dark, replaying the sound of her name in his mouth—Rosalind—like a piece of music she had been waiting her whole life to hear.

She did not know what she was becoming. She only knew that the north window was no longer enough, that the yard was no longer enough, that the looking had become a needing, and that somewhere above the horses there was a lantern that would burn for her, and that she would answer it.

The hayloft was theirs now. Nothing in the world had ever been hers before, and she fell asleep holding the ribbon against her heart, dreaming of a golden cave of straw and a boy who had taught himself the names of the stars.
