She knelt beside him, put her hand over the chart, over the ink coastline his finger had been tracing, and said, "Tell me."

"Tell you what?"

"Whatever you've been building in your head. I can hear it from here."

He looked at her a long moment, then turned the chart so she could see it — the bay below Blackwood, the headland, the cove marked in faded pencil where Ned Tarrant knew a man with a boat. "I've been thinking about the night of the ball," he said. "What comes after it. What could come after it."

The betrothal ball. Her father had fixed the date at last, a week before the wedding, and the household had gone into a stiff, frightened ferment of polish and whitewash, as if a coat of paint could make a sale look like a celebration. Rosalind had not let herself count the nights until it. But Callum had counted. Of course he had.

"The ball's at night," he said, low, his finger moving on the chart. "Every light in the house will be burning. Every servant will be in the kitchens or the hall. The stables will be empty — the one night in the year nobody'll be watching the horses. I can have two saddled before midnight, the two swiftest we've got, and waiting in the copse where the drive bends, out of sight of the house."

Her heart knocked against her ribs. "Waiting for what?"

"For you." He looked up, and his eyes were black and burning in the lamplight. "You slip away when the dancing's loudest. Down the back stairs, out the side door, across the yard — you know the way better than I do. I'll be in the copse with the horses. We ride for the coast along the old drovers' road, and we're at the cove by dawn. Ned's man will take us across. I've been saving, Rosalind. Coin enough for a passage and a week's bread on the far shore."

She stared at him. The words came out in a low, careful rush, the way a man speaks a thing he has been turning over in his mouth for days, and she understood he had been building it all his life, in the only way he knew how, and now he had the shape of it at last: a road, a cove, a boat, and her.

"You've been saving," she said faintly.

"Every penny Ned's paid me since I was twelve. I never knew what for. I think I was saving it for this. For a reason to spend it."

She took his face in her hands; the chart slid from his knees and neither noticed. "We'll be caught before the gate," she whispered. "They'll miss me before the last dance. My father will have every man in the county out by dawn—"

"Then we'll be past the county by dawn. The drovers' road's a day's ride at worst, and we'll be on it by midnight and at the sea by sunrise. They'll search inland, Rosalind — the way a lord's daughter would run, toward a town, toward something they understand. No one will think to look for us on the cliff road with the sea fog coming in. The fog hides everything. It's hidden us all spring."

"Elsie will raise the alarm when she comes to undress me—"

"I'll leave a note for Elsie." He said it simply, and she saw he had planned for everything, that this plan had been growing in him like a root under the floorboards, and he had only been waiting for her to be desperate enough to listen. "On your dressing table before I go to the copse. It'll say you're safe and gone by your own will, and that no one's to blame her for it, because she won't know where we've gone."

"And your life here." Her voice cracked. "Your horses. Ned. The only home you've ever had—"

"Is a loft above a stable in a house where I'm a thing that moves." He took her hands, and his were steady and warm, and hers were shaking. "The only home I've ever had is you, Rosalind. I'd rather live in a wet ditch on the far side of the sea with you than be master of Blackwood without you. And you said it yourself — you'd rather die on the road than be walked into that cage. Did you mean it?"

She had meant it in the dark of this very loft, with the ribbon against his heart and the Viscount's pale eyes behind her own. She looked at the chart, at the little cove, at the sea drawn in faded ink, and she felt something she had not felt in weeks: a bloom of hope, reckless and impossible, like a wild rose opening in dead winter.

"Yes," she said. "I meant it. When?"

"The night of the ball. Midnight. The copse where the drive bends." He squeezed her hands. "One week from tonight. We have one week to look like we're going along with it — you smile at your father, you let them fit the gown, you dance with the man they've sold you to. And every night, when the house sleeps, we come here and go over it again until we know it in our sleep. And then, at midnight, we run."

She kissed him with the wild rose blooming in her chest, and he kissed her back with the same desperate hope, and the lantern burned low, and below them the horses stamped, and for one week the world was theirs.

That was the week that followed — the brightest, most terrible week of Rosalind's life, terror and joy mixed until they were the same thing. She went through the days in a fever, playing her part with a skill that surprised her: she let Mrs. Haversham pin and measure her for the betrothal gown — white silk her father had ordered, cream roses at the bodice, a gown fit for a bride who was about to vanish — and she stood still through the fittings with her hands folded and her face pleasant, and all the while she was counting the copse, the road, the cove, the boat. She smiled at her father, and her father, who had not seen her smile in months, looked almost pleased, and she hated herself for the lie and could not stop it, because the lie was the door she was going to walk out of.

She ate, though the food sat in her stomach like stones, because a girl who fainted on the ride would be a girl who died on the ride. She told no one. That was the vow of the week: they spoke of the plan only in the hayloft, in the dark, where the fog swallowed their voices. In the yard Callum was the same stable hand touching his cap, and she was the same cold daughter walking past with her chin up, and the performance, which had once cost her everything, now cost her nothing, because she knew it was a performance — the real her was already riding the cliff road in her mind at all hours, feeling the wind and the speed and the sea ahead.

At night, in the loft, they went over it until it was real. The horses — a bay gelding called Bracken, swift and sure-footed, and a grey mare called Star, whom Callum trusted above all but Willow, too lame to take, and she watched him grieve that for the space of a breath and then let it go, because a man in love learns to leave even the things he loves. The route — the copse, the drovers' road, the long white ribbon of the cliff path, the descent to the cove at first light. The boat — Ned's man, a fellow called Purvis, who kept a herring boat in the lee of the headland and had carried fugitives for coin before, or so Ned said, and Ned's word was the best coin there was. The money — Callum counted it out on the sacking one night, a handful of silver and a few crumpled notes tied in oilcloth, eleven years of pennies, and she kissed his hands and did not weep, because she had promised herself she would not weep in that week, not once.

And the plan grew solid, a thing with weight, a door standing open at the end of a lit corridor. She began to believe it. That was the terrible, beautiful thing about that week: she believed it. She lay in her mother's bed and rehearsed the walk to the back stairs, the drop of the latch, the run across the yard with her heart going like a gull's — and she slept, actually slept, for the first time in weeks, dreaming of salt.

It was the note that undid her. In the loft, leaving a note for Elsie had seemed a kindness, a protection. But in the grey light of her room, with Elsie's hands in her hair and Elsie's careful voice asking whether my lady would wear the pearls or the sapphires, Rosalind found she could not bear it — could not leave the girl who had brushed her hair for seven years to find a cold note in the morning and stand before the Earl with the news of her own mistress's flight, innocent and friendless, while the whips came down.

"Elsie," Rosalind said, and her voice came out strange.

"My lady?"

"Lock the door."

Elsie's hands stilled. For a moment she did not move; then she crossed the room, turned the key, came back, and knelt at Rosalind's feet, her face carefully, terribly blank — the face of a servant who knows she is about to be told something she cannot unknow. And Rosalind saw that Elsie already knew. Not the shape of it, not the name, but the weight of it — she had been watching the fever, the muddied hems, the counted nights, the way her mistress had come alive and was now burning.

"There's no one else," Rosalind said. "There never has been. His name is Callum. He's the stable hand. We love each other, Elsie, in the way the world says we must not, and on the night of the ball we are going to ride for the coast and take a boat across the sea. I'm telling you so you won't find it out from a note on my table in the morning."

Elsie closed her eyes. The silence stretched so long Rosalind thought she had broken something in her; then Elsie opened them, wet, and said, "I knew. I didn't know the name of it, but I knew there was a someone. I saw it in your face last spring, my lady, the way you came back from the air looking fed, like a plant finally watered." She swallowed. "He's the one that saved the chestnut mare."

"Yes."

"They'll kill him." It was not a question. "And they'll put you in that carriage anyway."

"I know."

"And you'll go anyway."

"I'll go anyway."

Elsie looked at her for a long moment, then reached up and took Rosalind's hands and squeezed them. "Then I'll help you. I'll keep the bed turned down so it looks slept in. I'll tell anyone who asks that you were in your rooms all night, and I'll lie till I'm blue in the face and then I'll lie some more, and if they ever make me tell the truth, I'll have made sure it's too late for it to matter." She laughed a little, wet and broken. "He'd better be worthy of you."

"He is. He is the best man I have ever known."

"Then that's all I need to know." She pressed Rosalind's hands once more and let them go. "I'll bring you bread and dried meat for the ride, wrapped and hidden in the sideboard by the side door by tomorrow night. And I'll be at the window at midnight on the night of the ball, and I'll watch you go, and I'll be glad of it, and I'll never tell a living soul the part of it I know." She stood and smoothed her apron. "Now let me do your hair, my lady. It's a fine thing, to be going to a ball."

Rosalind told Callum that night that Elsie knew and was theirs, and she watched his face go through fear and then, slowly, wonder. "She's a good woman," he said at last. "You chose well. The world's full of people who'd sell what they know for a coin — Jem'll sell us for a story before the summer's out, mark me — and you found the one person in that house who wouldn't." He said it with reverence, and Rosalind's heart settled, and for one more night the door stood open and the wild rose burned.

But the world was already moving against them, and neither knew it. Four days before the ball, a horseman came up the drive at dusk — a stranger in a plain coat who asked at the kitchen door for water and a look at the stables, and who lingered, Rosalind learned later, asking the grooms about the horses, the roads, the tides, the boats at the cove. He was Wyndham's man. She did not know it then; she knew only that the horseman had a flat, measuring way of looking at things, like a man taking inventory, and that after he left, Callum was quieter, and the lantern burned lower, and the door in the corridor of her hope seemed, for a breath, to stand a little less open.

And in the servants' hall, a thin-faced boy with quick eyes had been watching everything for weeks and had begun, in his way, to count coin. He had seen the horseman's interest and the horseman's silver, and he had a story to sell and a grin like a man counting coin, and four days to decide which purse to sell it to.

Rosalind knew none of this. In the hayloft, on the last night before the ball, she lay in the hay with her head on Callum's shoulder and the rolled charts beside them and the lantern burning low, and she let herself have one hour of pure, unguarded hope, the wild rose in full and impossible bloom.

"The night after tomorrow," she whispered, "we'll be at sea. And the night after that we'll be somewhere on the far shore, and no one will know our names, and we'll be just a man and a woman who ran, and they can keep the county and the ball and the white silk and every cage in it."

He pressed his lips to her hair. "And I'll have the ribbon, and the knowing of you, and the sea, and the days. That's all I ever wanted, Rosalind. That was the whole of the dream, from the first night I saw you at the window. It was always you. It was only ever you."

Below them, somewhere in the dark, a horse stamped and the chain rattled, and the fog rolled in off the sea like a shroud — and neither of them heard, in the yard, the soft scrape of a boy's boot on the cobbles, or saw the quick bright eyes that had been watching the lantern, and counting coin, and making his choice.

The wild rose bloomed on in the dark one more night, and did not know the frost was already in the air.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth
set.description: Seventeen-year-old only daughter of the Earl of Ashworth; lives at Blackwood Hall in her late mother's rooms. The desperate plan is now fully built and believed: on the night of the betrothal ball (one week from tonight) she will slip out when the dancing is loudest, down the back stairs and out the side door, and meet Callum in the copse where the drive bends, then ride for the coast. This chapter she spent a feverish week performing compliance — smiling at her father (who looked almost pleased), standing still through fittings of the white silk betrothal gown with cream roses, eating to keep up strength — while rehearsing the run in her mind at all hours and sleeping dreaming of salt. She confided everything in Elsie, who swore to help. She still carries the knuckle of sea-glass in her pocket and sleeps with the mended sheepskin glove under her pillow; the blue ribbon is in Callum's keeping. Emotional state: hope blooming like a wild rose in dead winter, terror and joy mixed, a door standing open at the end of a lit corridor; she is unaware of the Viscount's spy or of Jem's watching. Location: Blackwood Hall, between her mother's rooms and the hayloft. Goal: survive the ball in disguise, reach the copse at midnight, and run for the sea with Callum.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: The Earl of Ashworth, a cold, prideful man who treats Rosalind as property and is performing fear for Viscount Wyndham, who holds his debts. The betrothal ball is fixed for one week before the wedding; he ordered a white silk gown with cream roses for Rosalind and was almost pleased by her sudden smiles, not suspecting the performance. He remains unaware of the plan, of Elsie's knowledge, of the spy in his own stable yard. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: keep Rosalind respectable through the betrothal ball and deliver her to Wyndham to preserve the Ashworth name.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's lady's maid, a quiet girl from the village with clever hands and a careful mouth. This chapter Rosalind locked the door and told her everything — Callum's name, the love the world forbids, the escape plan for the night of the ball. Elsie had already half-known ('I saw it in your face last spring... like a plant finally watered'); she swore to help: keep the bed turned down so it looks slept in, lie till she is blue in the face, hide bread and dried meat in the sideboard by the side door by the night before the ball, and watch from the window at midnight on the night of the ball and be glad of Rosalind's going. She has not yet been betrayed; she is now the one person who carries the full secret, which makes her the target the Viscount's spies will discover under threat of the whip (Ch. 10-11). Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing and Rosalind's rooms. Goal: serve her mistress by helping the escape and keeping the secret — a loyalty that will seal her doom.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old stable hand at Blackwood Hall, lean and dark with slate-dark hair and near-black guarded eyes; limps slightly on cold mornings; sleeps in a loft above the horses. This chapter he built the escape plan in full and unveiled it to Rosalind in the hayloft: on the night of the ball he will saddle the two swiftest horses — Bracken, a bay gelding, sure-footed, and Star, a grey mare he trusts above all but Willow (too lame to take, which he grieved for a breath and let go) — and wait in the copse where the drive bends out of sight of the house; they will ride the old drovers' road to the coast and be at the cove by dawn, where Purvis, the man Ned Tarrant knows, keeps a herring boat and will carry them across the sea. He has eleven years of saved pennies in oilcloth — enough for a passage and a week's bread on the far shore. He planned to leave a note for Elsie; Rosalind confided in Elsie directly instead. After the Viscount's spy came asking about roads, tides, and boats, Callum grew quieter and burned the lantern lower. He keeps the blue ribbon against his heart, the heather sprig on the ledge, and the sea charts. Location: Blackwood Hall stables and hayloft. Goal: keep the lantern burning through the last week, meet her in the copse at midnight on the night of the ball, and run for the sea.

In the hayloft, Callum unveiled the full escape plan: on the night of the betrothal ball, when every light in the house burns and the stables stand empty, he will saddle Bracken (a bay gelding, swift and sure-footed) and Star (a grey mare) and wait in the copse where the drive bends; Rosalind will slip away when the dancing is loudest, down the back stairs and out the side door; they will ride the old drovers' road to the coast, reach the cove by dawn, and take Purvis's herring boat (the man Ned Tarrant knows) across the sea. Callum has eleven years of saved pennies in oilcloth — enough for a passage and a week's bread on the far shore. The plan is set for midnight on the night of the ball, one week from the night it was devised.

A week before the ball, Rosalind locked her door and told Elsie everything: Callum's name, their forbidden love, and the escape plan. Elsie, who had long suspected a 'someone,' swore to help — she will keep the bed turned down to look slept in, lie for her mistress, hide bread and dried meat by the side door, and watch from the window at midnight on the night of the ball and be glad. This single act of trust makes Elsie the keeper of the secret and the one the Viscount's spies will discover and betray under threat of the whip.

Four days before the betrothal ball, a horseman in a plain coat came up the drive at dusk, asked at the kitchen door for water and a look at the stables, and lingered asking the grooms about the horses, the roads, the tides, and the boats at the cove. He was Viscount Wyndham's man. After he left, Callum grew quieter and burned the lantern lower; Rosalind did not know the man's purpose. The spy's report is the seed of the exposure at the ball.

Jem, the thin-faced quick-eyed groom's lad who watched Rosalind look too long at Callum in Ch. 6, saw the horseman's interest and silver and has been watching the lantern in the hayloft. He has a story to sell and a grin like a man counting coin, and four days to decide which purse to sell it to — the seed of the betrayal that will break the secret open at the betrothal ball.

The plan is set and must be attempted in Ch. 10: at midnight on the night of the betrothal ball, Rosalind slips down the back stairs and out the side door to the copse where the drive bends, where Callum waits with Bracken and Star, to ride the drovers' road to the cove and take Purvis's herring boat across the sea, with Elsie watching from the window and keeping the bed turned down. The attempt must be foiled when the stable doors burst open.

The Viscount's horseman-spy (who asked about roads, tides, and boats at the cove four days before the ball) and Jem the groom's lad (who has a story to sell and watched the lantern) must converge to betray the secret: Elsie will be discovered by the Viscount's spies and betrayed under threat of the whip, and the affair must break open at the betrothal ball (Ch. 10), leading to Callum's public flogging and exile (Ch. 11).

Elsie now carries the full secret of the escape. The Viscount's spies will discover her knowledge and she will be betrayed under threat of the whip, sealing the doom of the plan; her guilt afterwards (Ch. 12) will consume her.

chapters.name: The Betrothal Ball
chapters.content:
The day of the ball broke grey and cold, and by noon the whole of Blackwood Hall had the look of a corpse dressed for company.

Rosalind woke before the light, in her mother's bed, and lay very still with her heart pounding and her hands flat on the counterpane, rehearsing the night ahead the way she had rehearsed it every morning of the week: the back stairs, the side door, the yard, the copse where the drive bends. Callum would be there by midnight with Bracken and Star. She would be there before the last dance. The fog would roll in off the sea and hide them, the way it had hidden them all spring.

The dream was so close she could taste the salt on her lips before she had even risen.

Elsie came at first light and found her mistress already sitting at the window in her wrapper, watching the grey yard, and said nothing — only set down the tray and began to brush her hair with slow, steady strokes. Neither of them spoke of the sideboard in the servants' passage, where the bread and dried meat lay wrapped in a cloth. Neither spoke of the window at midnight, or the bed turned down to look slept in. Some things were too new and too precious to be said aloud in daylight, as if words could crack them.

"Mrs. Haversham will be up with the gown by nine," Elsie said at last. "It wants the last pin at the waist. Shall I tell her my lady is unwell?"

"No," Rosalind said. "Tell her I am well. Tell her I am very well. Tell everyone I am the happiest girl in England." She turned and smiled at Elsie, a real smile, strange and bright on a face grown used to other people's weather, and Elsie bent her head to the brushing, and her hands were not quite steady.

The gown was white silk, as her father had ordered, with cream roses worked at the bodice and sleeves, and when Rosalind stood in it before the long glass that afternoon she saw a stranger: a bride the world had made, pale and shining as a candle, with her mother's pearls at her throat and her hair pinned high with a white rose. She had never let herself be beautiful before. Now she looked at the stranger in the glass and thought, with a fierce, quiet joy, that this was the gown she would vanish in — that the county would remember Lady Rosalind Ashworth by this white silk, this perfect performance, and that by dawn the woman in the glass would be no one at all, a name no one knew, riding the cliff road toward the sea with the fog at her back.

Downstairs, the house was being dressed to die as well. The ballroom had been swept and whitewashed, the chandeliers strung with candles that would be lit at eight, the faded damask curtains replaced with borrowed hangings that smelled of other people's houses. Servants moved in a stiff, frightened quiet, polishing silver that had been sold twice already, arranging flowers that would wilt before midnight. Her father had spent money this week — money he did not have, on a night he could not afford — because the Viscount was coming, and the county was coming, and the sale had to look like a celebration.

Rosalind saw her father only once before the guests arrived. He came to the door of the morning room where she sat pretending to read, and stood looking at her with an expression she could not name — not pride, not love, something older and more tired, like a man checking that a painting had not fallen off the wall.

"You'll do credit to the house tonight," he said.

"I hope I shall, Papa."

He opened his mouth, closed it, and turned away; and she watched him go and felt, for the space of a breath, almost sorry for him — a man so small he had to sell his own daughter to keep a name that would not keep him. Then she remembered the pale eyes and the lattice of welts and the words my last wife, and the pity burned out of her like a spark in water.

The guests began to arrive at eight, and the candles were lit, and Blackwood Hall, which had gone grey and quiet for years, blazed like a lantern held up against the dark. Carriages came up the long drive in a procession of mud and torchlight; the county came in their best silks and their worst opinions, and the hall filled with the sound of false laughter and the smell of beeswax and cold perfume. Her father stood at the door receiving them, performing warmth with the desperation of a drowning man.

And then the black carriage came up the drive, and the room seemed to hold its breath.

Viscount Wyndham did not arrive so much as occupy. He came in dark blue, heavy and immovable, and the crowd parted before him the way water parts before a stone. He went straight to Rosalind, who stood with her mother's pearls at her throat and her heart gone suddenly, terribly cold, and he took her hand and raised it to his lips without bending to it — a salute, not a courtesy, the way a man handles a thing he owns.

"You look almost edible," he said, so only she could hear. "I detest girls who starve themselves for fashion. You'll do."

She smiled. It cost her everything, and she did it, and felt the performance like a blade in her palm, and thought of the copse, the road, the cove, the boat.

The dancing began. The music was a hired trio — violins and a cello that had played every ball in the county and knew better than to play anything that might make anyone feel anything — and the county couples moved through the figures with the mechanical grace of clockwork, smiling with dead eyes. Rosalind danced first with her father, who held her at arm's length as if she were a ledger he was balancing, and then with a succession of young men whose names she forgot between one set and the next, and through it all she counted: the minutes until midnight, the figures until the dancing grew loudest, the steps to the door.

And then the Viscount claimed her, and the world narrowed to his cold hand on her waist like a chain.

He danced well — of course he danced well, he did everything with the same flat, unhurried competence with which he bought horses and wives — and he held her closer than the figure required, his palm flat against the small of her back, steering her through the turns as if she were a mount he was schooling. She could smell the soap on him, the wine on his breath, the expensive wool of his coat. She kept her eyes on his cravat and counted his heartbeats and thought of the hayloft, of warm scarred hands, of a lantern burning low, and she smiled when the music required it and turned when his hand turned her and felt the minutes passing like coins dropping into a well.

"You're quiet tonight," he said, close to her ear. "A girl on the eve of her fortune is usually loud. I prefer the quiet ones. They cost less to keep."

"My lord," she said, "I am simply enjoying the evening."

"Mm." His thumb pressed once into the small of her back, a small private cruelty, a brand that said mine. "I've had your mare's temper looked at. That stable hand of yours, the dark one — he has opinions about horses. I don't keep men with opinions." He smiled, and it did not reach his pale eyes. "I'll want him gone by Michaelmas. I don't like the way he looks at things."

The words went into her like a splinter. She felt the blood drain from her face and made herself hold his gaze, made her voice steady, and said, "I'm sure you'll find him entirely useful, my lord, or entirely replaceable. The county is full of men who can groom a horse."

It was the right thing to say. He smiled a little less, and released her at the end of the set, and she curtsied and turned away before her legs could give out, and behind her the band struck up another tune, and the room swam.

She did not count the minutes after that. She simply waited, moving through the bright false room like a ghost, and the old clock above the stairs — the clock that had measured out her mother's dying and her own childhood — ticked toward the hour the way the tide ticks toward the shore.

At a quarter to midnight, she caught Elsie's eye across the crowded room. Elsie was carrying a tray of glasses, her face a careful blank, and for one moment their gazes met, and Elsie gave the smallest, almost imperceptible nod — the sideboard, the bread, the bed turned down, the window — and Rosalind felt her heart lift like a gull and knew that it was time.

She moved through the crowd with a smile, pausing to murmur a word to a countess, to laugh at a baron's joke, and no one noticed as she edged toward the door, because the dancing was at its loudest, the violins sawing at a country air, the floor a whirl of silk and candlelight. No one noticed when she slipped through the door into the dark corridor. No one noticed when she lifted her skirts and ran down the back stairs, past the kitchens where the servants were at their supper, out the side door into the black.

The night hit her like a wave — cold, wet, alive. The fog had come in off the sea, thick and white as wool, and the yard swam in it, the outbuildings blurred to ghosts. She ran across the cobbles with her heart going like a gull's, the white silk of the betrothal gown snapping around her ankles, and the fog swallowed her the way it had swallowed every secret of the spring, and she thought: I am free. I am actually free.

The copse where the drive bends was dark and dripping, the trees black against the white fog, and she did not see him until she was almost on top of them — the two horses, Bracken the bay and Star the grey, standing patient in the dark, their breath pluming, and Callum coming forward out of the mist with his face lit with a joy she had never seen on any face before.

She stopped. The world stopped. Everything she had rehearsed for a week fell away, and she stood in the fog in her white silk with her hair coming down, and he stood before her in his oldest coat with the whole of their life against his heart, and they looked at each other across three feet of wet grass and twelve years of a world that said no.

"Rosalind," he breathed. And then he reached out and took her hands, and their hands touched — his warm, callused, hers cold and shaking and alive — and for one breathtaking moment, the dream was within reach. The road. The cove. The boat. The far shore. A whole life, standing open in front of them like a door.

"Midnight," she said, and laughed, a wet, wild sound. "We made it. Callum, we actually made it."

"We made it." He squeezed her hands. "Come on. Star'll carry you — she's steadier than Bracken on a night like this—"

And then the stable doors burst open, and the lanterns blazed, and the dark came apart.

For one terrible, frozen second she did not understand what she was seeing. The stable yard, empty and fog-drowned a moment before, was suddenly full of men — a dozen of them, more, armed men in plain coats with lanterns and cudgels and the flat, familiar, taking-inventory look of the man who had come up the drive four days ago asking about roads and tides and boats. They came out of the fog like they had been waiting in it, and at their head, terrible and calm in the white light, walked Viscount Marcus Wyndham in his dark blue coat, with her father at his shoulder, grey-faced as a dead man, not looking at her.

And behind them, slipping out of the shadows with his thin face and his quick bright eyes and his grin like a man counting coin, came Jem.

"Callum," Rosalind said, and her voice came out small and strange, a girl's voice, the voice of the woman in the white silk who had almost been free.

Callum moved. He put himself between her and the light — that was the whole of his thinking, she understood it later, the whole of his body's plan — and he said, "Run," and she did not run, could not, her feet nailed to the wet grass by the sight of the armed men and the lanterns and the pale eyes.

"Ah," said the Viscount, stepping into the circle of light, his voice soft and satisfied, the voice of a man confirming a purchase. "The stable hand with the opinions. And the bride, out for a walk in her wedding gown. How touching."

Her father made a sound — a small, terrible sound, like a man being sick — and took a step toward her, and then stopped, and Rosalind looked at him, looked at his grey face and his shaking hands, and understood that there would be no help from that quarter, that there had never been any help from that quarter, that the world she had been born into and the world she was being sold into were the same world, and the cage had always been the same cage.

"Take the boy," the Viscount said. "And take the lady."

The men moved. Callum went down fighting — she saw him take the first man's cudgel blow on his forearm, saw him drive his shoulder into a second man and send him sprawling, saw him grab Star's rein and slap her flank and scream "Go! Go, go, go!" to the grey mare who stood rooted, terrified, not understanding — and then they were on him, three of them, four, dragging him down onto the wet cobbles, and she heard the sick sound of a boot in his ribs and she screamed, a sound she had never made in her life, a raw animal sound that cut through the fog and the lantern light and the false laughter of the ball still leaking faintly from the great house behind her.

"Callum! Callum!"

They had him. He was on his knees in the mud, his face bloodied, his arms pinned behind him, and the Viscount walked up to him slowly, the way he had walked up to the chestnut mare, and looked down at him with those pale, empty, satisfied eyes.

"You should have learned to want less," the Viscount said. And then, to the men, in the same flat tone: "Take him to the yard. Strip him. We'll finish this properly, before the whole house."

Rosalind was still screaming when they took her — two men on her arms, pulling her back toward the house, away from the mud and the lanterns and the boy kneeling in the wreckage of their door standing open. She fought them, clawed at them, heard her own voice begging, heard her father's voice saying her name, heard the Viscount's voice saying something about a whipping frame, and all of it came to her muffled and far away, as if through water.

The last thing she saw, as they dragged her through the side door and the fog swallowed the yard, was Callum's face lifted toward her in the lantern light — bloodied, wrecked, and somehow still full of her, his eyes holding hers across the whole terrible distance of the yard, saying without words, with everything he had, the thing he had said every night of the spring: the lantern burns. The knowing is kept. Whatever they do to me, Rosalind — run. Keep running.

And then the door closed, and the fog closed, and the dream closed, and the night of the ball went on inside the house, glittering and hollow, the violins sawing on, the false laughter rising — and in the stable yard, in the lantern light, under the eyes of the assembled household summoned to watch, they stripped the stable boy to the waist and began.

Somewhere above, in the dark of her mother's room, behind a locked door, Rosalind Ashworth stood at the window in her ruined white silk, her fists pressed to the glass, and screamed until her voice was gone — and the ball played on, and the candles burned, and the fog rolled in off the sea like a shroud, and nothing in all the world heard her at all.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth
set.description: Seventeen-year-old only daughter of the Earl of Ashworth; imprisoned in her mother's locked rooms at Blackwood Hall after the escape was foiled at the betrothal ball. She wears the ruined white silk betrothal gown with cream roses, torn and muddied from the copse, her hair down, her mother's pearls at her throat. In the copse at midnight she met Callum with Bracken and Star and their hands touched — then Wyndham's armed men burst from the yard with lanterns and cudgels, the Viscount and her grey-faced father at their head, Jem slipping out of the shadows with his counting-coin grin. She saw Callum fight and be beaten down onto the cobbles, heard the Viscount order him stripped and whipped before the household, was dragged back through the side door screaming and locked in her room, where she stood at the window pounding the glass and screaming until her voice was gone while the whipping began in the yard and the ball played on. She still carries the knuckle of sea-glass in her pocket; the mended sheepskin glove is under her pillow; the blue ribbon is in Callum's keeping. Emotional state: shock and despair, the door slammed shut, grief and terror mixed with a stubborn refusal to stop loving him; she does not yet know if he is alive. Location: locked room (her mother's rooms), Blackwood Hall. Goal: watch from the window through the night; refuse food and speech in the days ahead (Ch. 12); her hope is broken but her vow holds.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: The Earl of Ashworth, cold, prideful, performing fear of Viscount Wyndham, who holds his debts. At the betrothal ball he received the county with desperate false warmth, spent money he did not have to make the sale look like a celebration, and stood grey-faced at the Viscount's shoulder as the armed men foiled the escape in the copse, took Callum, and dragged Rosalind back to her room; he made one small terrible sound and did nothing. He will permit Callum's public flogging and exile to proceed before the assembled household and keep Rosalind locked in her rooms while wedding preparations continue. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: preserve the Ashworth name by delivering Rosalind to Wyndham whatever the cost; the last of his feeling for her died the night he let them take her.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's lady's maid, a quiet girl from the village with clever hands and a careful mouth; the only one who carried the full secret of the escape. At a quarter to midnight she caught Rosalind's eye across the crowded ballroom and gave the smallest nod — the bread and dried meat in the sideboard, the bed turned down to look slept in, the watch at the window — and saw her mistress slip out. She now knows the escape failed, that Callum was taken and beaten, that Rosalind was dragged back and locked in her rooms, and that the household is being assembled for Callum's flogging. She still carries the secret and has not yet been discovered, but her guilt is already beginning to consume her. Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing. Goal: protect her mistress; she will be found out by the Viscount's men and betrayed under threat of the whip (Ch. 11-12), and her guilt will break her.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old stable hand at Blackwood Hall, lean and dark with slate-dark hair and near-black guarded eyes; in custody in the stable yard after the escape was foiled at the ball. He waited in the fog-dark copse with Bracken (bay gelding) and Star (grey mare), took Rosalind's hands, and for one breathtaking moment the dream was within reach — then Wyndham's armed men burst from the yard with lanterns and cudgels, the Viscount, the Earl, and Jem the groom's lad at their heels. He put himself between Rosalind and the light, told her to run, fought, took a cudgel blow on his forearm, and was dragged down onto the cobbles, bloodied, his ribs booted, his arms pinned; he slapped Star's flank to drive her off but the grey mare stood rooted in terror. The Viscount said 'You should have learned to want less' and ordered him stripped to the waist and whipped before the assembled household on a whipping frame. He kept the blue ribbon hidden against his heart; his last look at Rosalind carried the old vow — the lantern burns, the knowing is kept, run. Location: Blackwood Hall stable yard, in custody, awaiting the public flogging. Goal: survive the flogging and the exile on pain of death (Ch. 11), keep the ribbon and the knowing of Rosalind.

On the night of the betrothal ball Rosalind slipped away at a quarter to midnight (Elsie nodded from across the room), ran through the fog to the copse where the drive bends, and met Callum with Bracken and Star saddled. Their hands touched and for one moment the dream was within reach — then the stable doors burst open and Wyndham's armed men flooded the yard with lanterns and cudgels, the Viscount and the grey-faced Earl at their head, and Jem slipping out of the shadows with his counting-coin grin. Callum fought, was beaten down onto the cobbles and pinned; the Viscount said 'You should have learned to want less' and ordered him stripped and whipped before the household. Rosalind was dragged back through the side door, locked in her mother's rooms in her ruined white silk, and screamed at the window while the ball played on and the flogging began in the yard.

During their dance at the betrothal ball, Viscount Wyndham pressed his thumb once into the small of Rosalind's back like a brand and told her he had had her mare's temper looked at, that the dark stable hand 'has opinions about horses,' that he does not keep men with opinions, and that he will want Callum gone by Michaelmas. Rosalind answered that the county is full of men who can groom a horse. This is the Viscount's private signal that he has been watching the stable yard and that Callum's fate was already decided before the ambush.

Jem, the thin-faced quick-eyed groom's lad who watched Rosalind look too long at Callum, made his choice and sold his story to the Viscount's men: he came out of the shadows at the copse behind the armed party, grinning like a man counting coin, his betrayal the final thread that broke the secret open at the betrothal ball.

Callum is in custody, stripped to the waist in the stable yard with the assembled household watching; Ch. 11 must open with the public flogging (cat-o'-nine-tails) and the Earl pronouncing exile from Blackwood Hall on pain of death, while Rosalind watches from her locked window and is dragged away, then sees him stumble down the long road into the fog.

Rosalind is now locked in her mother's rooms at Blackwood Hall in her ruined white silk; in Ch. 12 she will refuse food and speech while wedding preparations proceed below, and Elsie, discovered and betrayed under threat of the whip, will confess her part.

chapters.name: The Reckoning
chapters.content:
The whipping frame stood in the middle of the stable yard, where the maypole had stood in Rosalind's childhood, and the sight of it through the fog-wet window glass was so wrong, so obscenely ordinary, that for a moment she could not understand what she was seeing.

It was an old thing, dragged from the tool shed where it had rotted for thirty years — two oak posts and a crossbeam, iron rings bolted to the wood, rust flaking off them like dried blood. Torches had been jammed between the cobbles in a ring around it, and their flames beat against the fog, throwing a circle of sick orange light over the yard. Around that circle stood the household: every servant Blackwood had ever kept, summoned from their beds and their suppers, pressed shoulder to shoulder against the stable block and the kitchen wing, their faces white discs in the torchlight. Cook stood with her apron twisted into ropes in her fists. Mrs. Haversham had her hand pressed over her mouth. Ned Tarrant stood at the front, grey and still as a post, his face like a door that had been closed and locked from the inside.

And in the middle of the circle, wrists tied to the crossbeam, back bare to the flames, stood Callum.

Rosalind pressed her forehead to the cold glass and could not look away, and could not look, and could not look away.

They had taken his shirt. It lay in the mud at the foot of the frame, a grey rag, and she saw with a strange, drowning clarity the way the torchlight moved over his shoulders, over the working muscles of his back, over the scars she knew by heart from the hayloft — the pale line across his ribs where a horse had kicked him as a boy, the burn on his shoulder blade from the forge. She had traced those scars in the warm straw, in the dark, when the world had been theirs. Now the same back was offered up to the flames and the crowd like a page of writing, and there was nothing of her in it, nothing of the hayloft, nothing of the spring.

One of Wyndham's men stood beside the frame with the cat-o'-nine-tails coiled in his fist — a short, thick-hafted thing with nine knotted cords, each cord weighted at the end. He tested it once against the post, a lazy, practiced flick, and the crack snapped across the yard like a shot, and some of the servants flinched and some of them did not, and the fog seemed to swallow the sound and give it back doubled.

The Viscount stood at the edge of the circle in his dark blue coat, arms folded, patient as a man watching a horse shod. Her father stood beside him, grey-faced, not looking at anything, his hands clasped so tight before him that his knuckles showed white.

"Thirty strokes," the Viscount said pleasantly, to no one in particular, as if he were ordering wine. "The usual tariff for a groom who forgets his place. Cut his shirt off him and begin."

Two men went to the frame. Rosalind saw them take hold of the grey shirt and rip it down the middle, and she saw Callum flinch — not at the flogging, which had not yet begun, but at the taking of the shirt, and she understood why in the same instant she saw it: something blue fell from the torn cloth and tumbled into the mud at his feet.

The ribbon. Her ribbon. The one she had tied in her hair every day of the spring, the one he had kissed and folded and tucked against his heart the night the Viscount came, the one he had sworn to keep till he died and after.

One of the men stooped and scooped it out of the mud with two fingers, holding it up to the torchlight, a sodden twist of faded blue. "What's this, then? A keepsake?" He grinned around the yard. "Groom's got himself a sweetheart. We should've whipped him for that alone."

Callum said something she could not hear — a single hoarse word — and the man laughed, and tossed the ribbon at him, and she watched Callum catch it one-handed, his wrists still free before the binding, and she watched him tie it around his own wrist, clumsy and quick, knotting it with his teeth, and she saw the Viscount watch this with a pale, narrow amusement and say nothing, and she knew with a sick certainty that the Viscount understood exactly what the ribbon was, and was choosing, for his own reasons, to let it stay.

"Tie him," the Viscount said.

They tied him. They bound his wrists to the crossbeam above his head, and his body took the strain, and the torchlight ran over the ruined shirt in the mud and the blue ribbon on his wrist, and the man with the whip stepped back and settled his feet, and the yard went still.

"No," Rosalind said, and heard her own voice as if from very far away, a thin broken sound against the glass. "No, no, no—" and she beat her fists against the window, and the glass shuddered, and no one in all that fog-bound yard turned their face toward the dark window of her mother's room.

The first stroke fell.

It made a sound she had never heard in her life and would never be able to unhear: a wet, whistling crack, and then Callum's whole body bowed against the ropes, his head thrown back, and he made no sound at all. The man counted, flat and bored. "One." And raised the whip again.

She clawed at the window latch, but it was painted shut, sealed by generations of damp, and she tore her nails on it and did not feel it, and through the glass she watched the second stroke fall, and the third, and the count went up like a litany — four, five, six — and Callum's back began to change, to bloom, to come apart in long red welts that crossed and recrossed like the grain of a plank, and still he made no sound, and she understood, with a horror beyond grief, that he was holding the sound inside himself on purpose, that he would not give them the pleasure of it, that even now he was protecting something — her, the secret, the small blue knot on his wrist, the only things in the world he had ever dared to want.

Seven. Eight. The crowd had gone utterly silent. She could see Elsie in the press of servants, her hand pressed to her mouth, her eyes wet and enormous, and beside her stood a plain-coated man — one of the Viscount's men, she recognized the flat, taking-inventory look — and he was not watching the whipping at all. He was watching Elsie. He was watching the way she shook, the way her lips moved in a silent litany of her own, the way her eyes went, again and again, to the dark window where Rosalind stood, and away.

And Rosalind, through the roaring in her ears, through the count — nine, ten, eleven — understood suddenly, with a cold horror that had nothing to do with the flogging, that Elsie's face had already given her away, that the secret was bleeding out of her in front of every watching eye, and that there was nothing she could do to stop it, because she was locked in a room thirty feet above the yard and the boy she loved was being taken apart by inches below her.

Twelve. Thirteen. She could see blood now, dark and shining, running down the furrows of his back and soaking into the waistband of his breeches, and still the man counted, and still the whip rose and fell, and still Callum did not scream. His face was turned toward the house — toward her window, she saw, she saw it with a lurch of her heart — and his eyes were open and fixed on the dark glass where she stood, and she knew, with a terrible and perfect knowledge, that he had found her in the dark. That he was holding her with his eyes the way he had held her in the hayloft, the way he had held her in the copse, and that he was telling her, with everything he had left, the same thing he had told her every night of the spring: the lantern burns. The knowing is kept. Whatever they do to me — run.

"Stop!" she screamed, and the word came out as a raw croak, her voice already gone. "Stop it, stop it, stop it—" and she threw herself at the door, and it was locked, of course it was locked, and she beat her fists against the panels until her knuckles split, and the count went on below her — sixteen, seventeen, eighteen — and the sound of the whip was like something breaking inside her, over and over, in the exact rhythm of her own heart.

And then — she never understood afterward how it happened, whether the old lock had failed, whether the door had simply given way under the force of a body gone mad with grief — the door flew open, and she was through it, and running.

She ran down the long corridor of her mother's rooms in her ruined white silk, her hair down, her hands bleeding, past the portrait of her mother smiling in her youth, down the back stairs, through the kitchen passage where the servants' supper stood abandoned and cold, and out through the side door into the fog and the torchlight and the yard, and the crowd parted before her like water, and she saw the frame, and she saw Callum, and she saw the ruin of his back, and she screamed.

She did not know what she screamed. She only knew that she reached them — her father and the Viscount stood so close together in the torchlight, two men appraising the same merchandise — and she clawed at them, at her father's coat, screaming "Stop it, stop it, you can't, you can't—" and her father caught her wrists, held her off with a strength she had not known he possessed, and looked at her, and his face was grey and wet, and he said her name once, "Rosalind," in a voice she had never heard from him, a voice with nothing left in it at all.

"Papa," she sobbed, "Papa, please, I'll do anything — I'll marry him, I'll marry anyone, I'll be good, I'll be silent, I'll be whatever you want, only please, Papa, please make them stop—"

Behind her, very calmly, the Viscount said: "Twenty-six."

Her father's hands tightened on her wrists, and she saw something move in his face — a muscle jumping in his jaw, his eyes going to the frame, to the boy hanging from it, to the Viscount, to the assembled household, to her — and she thought, for one wild, terrible moment, that he was going to do it. That he was going to stop this. That somewhere inside the man there remained a corner that remembered he had once had a daughter, a wife, a heart.

And then his grip slackened, and he let her go, and he turned his face away, and he said to the men who were already at her shoulders — of course they were there, two of the Viscount's men, waiting — "Take her back. Lock her in."

"Papa—"

"Take her back," he said, to the men, not to her, his voice flat and dead as a ledger, "and lock her in. And if she comes out again before morning, it will be the whip for whoever let her."

She was lifted off her feet. She fought them, clawed and kicked and screamed his name and her father's name and Callum's name, and the last thing she saw before the side door swallowed her was Callum's face turned toward her over his shoulder, blood running down his ribs, his eyes still holding her, his lips forming a word she could not hear but knew with all her heart.

Run.

The door slammed. She was carried up the stairs, and the door of her mother's room slammed behind her, and she heard the key turn, and she stood in the dark with her chest heaving and her hands bleeding and her voice gone, and below, through the floor, she heard the count continue — twenty-eight, twenty-nine — and then a long silence.

And then the voice of the man with the whip, flat and final: "Thirty."

She was at the window before she knew she had moved, her palms pressed to the glass, and she watched them cut him down.

He fell. He went to his knees in the mud at the foot of the frame, his hands going to the earth, and she saw him try to stand, and she saw his legs buckle, and she saw him try again, and she saw Ned Tarrant step forward — old Ned, who had found him on the moor road eleven years ago with his ribs showing and his feet wrapped in rags — and she saw Ned reach out a hand, and she saw one of the Viscount's men put a palm on Ned's chest and push him back, and she saw Ned's face, and she had to look away.

Her father's voice rose over the yard, carrying up to her window through the fog, and it was the voice he had used in his study the day he told her about the debts, the voice of a man reading numbers aloud: "Callum, late of the Blackwood stables. For the crime of laying hands on a lady of this house. For the crime of ambition. You are hereby exiled from Blackwood Hall and its lands, on pain of death. You will not return. You will not write. You will not be named. If you are found on this ground again, you will be shot like a dog. This house is done with you. Go."

There was a silence. She watched a man pick up the grey rag of Callum's shirt and toss it at him, and she watched Callum catch it one-handed, and she watched him stand. He stood. She would remember that for the rest of her life, she would — he stood, swaying, his back a ruin, his face white and running with blood and sweat, and he stood, and he looked up once at the dark window where she stood with her hands pressed to the glass, and his lips moved, and she could not hear the words, but she knew them as surely as she knew the shape of her own name: the lantern burns. The knowing is kept. And then he turned, and he walked.

They drove him out through the yard gate and onto the long road, and the fog swallowed him to the knees, to the waist, to the shoulders, and he went down the road in the white dark, stumbling, one arm wrapped around his ribs, his back laid open and bleeding, and she watched him go, and she did not take her eyes off him, and at the very last, just before the fog closed over him completely, she saw it — a flicker of blue at his wrist, the ribbon he had tied there, the only color left in all the grey world, going down the road away from her, and then the fog closed, and the road was empty, and the world was empty, and she stood at the window in her mother's room with the ruined white silk of the betrothal gown pooled at her feet and her mother's pearls cold against her throat, and she watched the empty road until the fog was all there was.

Somewhere below she heard the household disperse in a shuffle of feet and hushed whispers. She heard the Viscount's carriage horses stamp and jingle. She heard her father's voice and the Viscount's voice, low and satisfied, speaking of the wedding and the date, of settlements and seasons. She heard them all, muffled, as if through water.

She did not move.

She stood at the window until the torches burned down and guttered out, one by one, and the fog thinned and thickened and thinned again, and the first grey light of a false dawn crept over the moors, and the road stayed empty, and the sea beyond the moors stayed grey, and the place where Callum had been stayed empty, and she put her hand to the glass and wrote his name there with her fingertip in the steam of her own breath, and the name faded, and she wrote it again, and it faded, and she wrote it again, and she was still writing it, her knuckles bloody, her voice a memory, when Elsie came to the door in the grey morning and found her there, and did not speak, and set down the tray of food that Rosalind would not touch, and stood behind her in the cold room and wept without a sound, because there was nothing left in all the world that either of them could say.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth
set.description: Seventeen-year-old only daughter of the Earl of Ashworth; locked in her mother's rooms at Blackwood Hall on the grey morning after the betrothal ball. She wears the ruined white silk betrothal gown with cream roses, torn and muddied, her hair down, her mother's pearls cold at her throat. During the night she broke out of the locked room, ran down to the yard mid-flogging, clawed at her father and begged — offering to marry anyone if he would make them stop — was dragged back by the Viscount's men and locked in again; the Earl threatened the whip for whoever let her out. From the window she watched the whole reckoning: the whipping frame, thirty strokes of the cat-o'-nine-tails on Callum's bare back, his silence through the count, the blue ribbon falling from his torn shirt and his tying it around his wrist, the Earl pronouncing exile on pain of death, and Callum stumbling down the long road into the fog until the fog swallowed the last flicker of blue at his wrist. She also saw one of the Viscount's men watching Elsie rather than the whipping, and understood the secret was bleeding out of Elsie in front of everyone. She screamed until her voice was gone; her knuckles are split from beating the door and the glass; she wrote his name on the window glass in her breath through the night. She refused the tray of food Elsie set down. She still carries the knuckle of sea-glass in her pocket; the mended sheepskin glove is under her pillow; the blue ribbon is now in exile with Callum. Emotional state: beyond tears into a stunned, watchful numbness; her vow to keep loving him holds; she does not know if he will live or die on the road. Location: locked room (her mother's rooms), Blackwood Hall. Goal: refuse food and speech in the days ahead (Ch. 12), watch the empty road, keep him alive in her own heart; hope broken but the vow unbroken.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: The Earl of Ashworth, cold, prideful, performing fear of Viscount Wyndham, who holds his debts. At the flogging he stood grey-faced at the Viscount's shoulder, held Rosalind's wrists when she clawed at him mid-whipping, let the Viscount's men take her, gave the order to lock her in again and threatened the whip for whoever let her out, then pronounced the sentence of exile before the assembled household — 'on pain of death, you will not return, you will not write, you will not be named' — and afterwards stood with the Viscount discussing the wedding date, settlements and seasons in low satisfied tones. The last of his feeling for his daughter died the night he let them take her; his voice when he read the sentence was the flat dead voice of a man reading numbers. Location: Blackwood Hall, overseeing wedding preparations. Goal: preserve the Ashworth name by delivering Rosalind to Wyndham whatever the cost, now that the sale is sealed and the boy is gone.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's lady's maid, a quiet village girl with clever hands and a careful mouth, the only one who carried the full secret of the escape. She witnessed Callum's flogging from the press of servants and wept openly, her lips moving in a silent litany, her eyes going again and again to Rosalind's dark window — and one of the Viscount's men watched her instead of the whipping, marking her with a flat taking-inventory look as the keeper of the secret. In the grey morning she brought food to Rosalind's locked door, which Rosalind refused; she stood behind her mistress in the cold room and wept without a sound. Her guilt is consuming her; her face already gave her away. Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing and Rosalind's door. Goal: protect her mistress; she will be discovered and betrayed under threat of the whip (Ch. 12), and her guilt will break her into confession.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old former stable hand of Blackwood Hall, now exiled: tied to the whipping frame in the torch-lit yard and given thirty strokes of the cat-o'-nine-tails, his back laid open, his ribs already bruised from boots, his face bloodied — and he made no sound through the whole count, holding it inside on purpose so as not to give them the pleasure. When his shirt was torn from him the blue ribbon fell into the mud; he caught it and tied it around his wrist, and the Viscount, understanding what it was, let it stay. After the thirtieth stroke he was cut down, refused to stay down, stood swaying, took his torn shirt, looked up once at Rosalind's window and mouthed the old vow — the lantern burns, the knowing is kept — and was driven out through the yard gate down the long road into the fog, stumbling, one arm around his ribs, bleeding, on pain of death if he ever returns. He carries the grey rag of his shirt and the blue ribbon at his wrist and almost nothing else; the fate of the oilcloth of saved pennies is uncertain. Location: exiled, on the long road out of Blackwood Hall into the fog. Goal: survive the road and the wound, keep the ribbon and the knowing of Rosalind, never set foot on Ashworth ground again on pain of death.

Before the assembled household in the torch-lit stable yard, Callum was tied to the whipping frame and given thirty strokes of the cat-o'-nine-tails, his back laid open; he made no sound through the count, holding it inside to deny them the pleasure. The Earl then pronounced the sentence: exile from Blackwood Hall and its lands on pain of death — he will not return, will not write, will not be named, and will be shot like a dog if found on the ground again. Callum stood, took his torn shirt, and was driven out the yard gate down the long road into the fog, bleeding and stumbling.

Midway through the flogging Rosalind broke out of her locked room, ran down through the house and into the torch-lit yard, clawed at her father's coat and begged — offering to marry anyone, to be good and silent, if he would make them stop. The Earl held her wrists, then let go, turned his face away, and ordered the Viscount's men to take her back and lock her in, threatening the whip for whoever let her out. Her voice broke from screaming and her knuckles split.

During the flogging, one of the Viscount's plain-coated men watched Elsie rather than the whipping — her weeping, her shaking, her eyes going again and again to Rosalind's dark window — marking her as the keeper of the secret. The secret is bleeding out of her and the Viscount's people now have their eye on her; seed of her discovery and betrayal under threat of the whip (Ch. 12).

The blue ribbon passed into exile: when Callum's shirt was torn from him before the flogging, the ribbon fell into the mud, he caught it and tied it around his wrist, and it went down the long road into the fog with him — the last color Rosalind saw before the fog closed. The ribbon remains in Callum's keeping so that it can be returned to her after his death in a far coastal village (Ch. 19).

The faded blue ribbon now goes into exile tied around Callum's wrist, the last color Rosalind saw before the fog closed over the long road. It must be returned to Rosalind after his death in a far coastal village across the sea, wrapped in oilskin with a priest's note (Ch. 19), the final relic of their love.

One of the Viscount's men marked Elsie at the flogging, watching her instead of the whipping. She will be discovered and betrayed under threat of the whip, and her guilt will break her into confessing her part to Rosalind (Ch. 12).

chapters.name: The Prisoner
chapters.content:
The days after the fog closed over the long road were the longest of Rosalind's life, and they were all the same day.

She did not count them. Counting was a thing of before, of the spring, when she had known the shape of a week by the nights the lantern burned and the mornings she crossed the yard. Now there was only the grey light at the window and the grey dark, and the empty road, and the sea beyond the moors that stayed grey, and the name she wrote on the glass with her fingertip in the steam of her own breath, over and over, until the glass was cloudy and her finger was raw and the name faded and she wrote it again.

Callum.

She did not know if he was alive. That was the thought that came to her in the small hours, when the hammering had stopped and the house was silent — whether he had made it to a barn, a ditch, a shepherd's hut; whether the bleeding had stopped or whether he had lain down somewhere on the moor road and not got up again; whether he had died with her name in his mouth and the blue ribbon tied around his wrist, or whether he was walking still, one arm around his ribs, down a road she would never see. She did not know. She would never know. That was the true shape of the prison they had put her in: not the locked door, not the barred window, but the not-knowing.

The food came and went. Elsie set the tray on the floor inside the door, and Rosalind did not look at it, and Elsie carried it away untouched and brought another. The smell of it — broth, bread, preserves — filled the room and sickened her. She drank water from the ewer when thirst grew too great, and that was all. Her body began to feel like something she was merely carrying, light and hollow, and she found she did not care.

Her father did not come.

She had thought, in the first hours, that he would. That he would open the door and say something she could hold onto, some crack in the wall of his silence through which she might see the man who had once lifted her onto a pony, whose hand she had held at her mother's funeral. He did not come. Instead, on the second day, she heard his voice outside the door — not for her, but for Mrs. Haversham, who had come with a measuring tape and a mouth full of pins. The words came through the panels muffled and flat: the wedding was set for the first Sunday after the harvest moon; the Viscount's man had ridden with the settlements; the village seamstress would be brought up to take her measurements in the morning. "She will cooperate," her father said, and it was not a hope but a fact. "She will wear what she is given. See to it."

Rosalind stood very still in the middle of the room and listened to his footsteps recede, and she understood that there would be no crack. The man who had held her wrists in the torchlight and let her go, whose jaw had jumped and whose eyes had gone to the boy on the frame — that man had drowned in the fog, and what remained was the Earl, and the Earl had already spent her.

She refused the measurements. When Mrs. Haversham came with the tape and the pins and the soft, careful voice, Rosalind stood at the window with her back to the door and did not turn around, and did not answer, and at last the footsteps retreated and the key turned again. Later she heard her father's voice in the corridor, low and cold: "She will not be fed until she cooperates. Let her starve a day and see how her pride fares." She heard Mrs. Haversham's small sound of protest, and her father's "It is done. She has had her chance to be a daughter."

The food stopped coming.

She was not hungry. It was the strange mercy of it — her body had gone past hunger into a place where food was only an idea that no longer concerned her. She stood at the window and watched the road. She watched the servants cross the yard, heads down; none of them looked up at her window, not one, and she could not blame them, because she had heard the threat of the whip for whoever let her out, and fear is a cheap thing to buy a whole household with, and her father had bought them all.

On the third day she saw Ned Tarrant. He came out of the stable block in the grey afternoon and stood in the yard, holding a bridle he was not mending, and he did not look up at her window, but he stood there a long time, where he could be seen, in case she was watching. She watched him until the light failed and he turned and went back inside, and she pressed her hand to the glass and thought: he is alive. Ned would not stand like that if the boy were dead.

On the fourth night, Elsie said, "He got away. I heard Ned tell Cook. He got to the cove — Purvis's boat is gone from its mooring, and the oilcloth of pennies is gone with it. Ned thinks he took it, or someone took him. He's out of the county, miss. He's free."

And Rosalind, who had not spoken in four days, turned from the window for the first time and looked at her, and Elsie's face crumpled and she put her hand over her mouth and wept, and Rosalind looked at her a long time, and then turned back to the window, and the not-knowing in her chest loosened by a single thread, and she thought: he is free. He is free, and he is gone, and I will never see him again, and he is free.

That was the night Elsie broke.

She had stood in the dark behind her mistress, and she said the words she had been carrying since the yard, the words that had been eating her alive, in a rush, as if she were afraid she could not say them if she stopped.

"It was me. Miss Rosalind, it was me. They came for me two days before the ball — the Viscount's man, the one in the plain coat. He found me in the kitchen passage and told me they knew everything, that my face had given it all away at the whipping, that they'd take me to the frame and put the cat on my back the way they'd done to him, unless I told them when and where. And I was so afraid. I've never been so afraid. I thought if I told them, they'd only stop you, they'd lock you in and it would be over and the boy would live — I thought the boy would live—"

Her voice broke, and she went on, because there was no stopping now. "I told them the copse, and the horses, and the hour. I told them everything. And they still whipped him — and it was my words that put him on that frame, my words that put your hands through that glass—"

She fell to her knees. Rosalind heard the soft, terrible sound of a person crumpling, heard Elsie's forehead knock against the floorboards, heard her weeping into her apron. "Do what you like to me. I'd rather the whip than this. I'd rather anything than your silence, miss, because your silence is worse than any whip."

Rosalind stood at the window with her back to the room and listened, and the words went into her one by one, each a small cold thing, and she felt something in her chest — the thing that had held the spring, the lantern, the ribbon — begin to close, like a fist, like a door. She understood it now. The plain-coated man had not merely marked Elsie at the flogging; he had been reading her, and her face had told him everything, and by the time the ball came they had not needed Jem's counting-coin grin at all. The secret had bled out of Elsie in the torchlight while Rosalind stood locked above, and there had been nothing anyone could do to stop it.

She turned.

Elsie was on the floor at her feet, a heap of grey wool and shaking shoulders, her face hidden. And Rosalind found — this surprised her, this was the last thing she had expected — that she did not hate her. She could not. The girl on the floor had not chosen cruelty; she had chosen fear, and fear was the only coin this house had ever paid anyone in, the same as Callum, the same as Ned, the same as every soul who slept in the attics while the Ashworths slept in the damp silk of their inheritance. Elsie had not put Callum on the frame. The men who had put him there had stood in the torchlight and counted.

The anger did not come. What came instead was a wound — a clean, deep wound where the fury should have been, a place that would not close, that would not even bleed, that simply was. Her heart hardened into that wound and went on beating around it, and she looked down at Elsie and felt a great grey tiredness, and the knowledge that the girl had carried this for four days, and that carrying it had already flogged her more thoroughly than any whip.

"Get up," Rosalind said.

Her voice came out rusted, unused, dragged up from the bottom of a well. Elsie flinched as if she had been struck.

"Miss—"

"Get up," Rosalind said again. "You brought me news. You told me he is free. That is worth something. It may be worth everything." The words came slowly, like water through sand. "You were afraid. This house has made you afraid since you were a child. It made him afraid too, and he chose to be brave anyway, and you chose to be afraid instead, and I will not pretend those are the same. But I will not see you whipped for it, and I will not see you damned for it, because I have seen the men who deserve the damning, and they are not in this room."

Elsie stared up at her, tear-streaked, disbelieving.

"Water," Rosalind said. "Bring me the water. And then go, and sleep, and do not come back tonight."

Elsie rose on shaking legs. She brought the ewer and set it in Rosalind's hands, her fingers cold and trembling, and Rosalind looked down at her own hands holding it, at the split knuckles beginning to heal, and she said, to Elsie, and to the empty room, and to the grey window, and to no one:

"Whatever they do to me, I will not stop loving him. That is the one thing they cannot take. It is the only thing I have left."

Elsie left. The key turned. Rosalind stood alone in her mother's room with the ewer in her hands, and below her, through the floor, she heard the hammering of the workmen, and the laughter of the maids, and her father's voice giving orders about flowers and favors and the first Sunday after the harvest moon, and she set the ewer down and went back to the window, and watched the empty road, and began, again, to write the name on the glass.

She did not know if he was alive. She would go on not knowing, maybe for the rest of her life. But the not-knowing was no longer the whole of her prison — she had given herself to it, and then she had taken herself back, a small and stubborn theft, the only one left to her. The spirit could drain and drain and leave her hollow, and they would dress her in white and walk her down an aisle she had not chosen, and the Viscount would put his cold hand on her waist, and she would endure it, because endurance was the only shape her love could take now — a shape no one in that house could see, a shape no whip could reach.

Below, the wedding preparations proceeded. Above, in the grey light, the road stayed empty, and the sea stayed grey, and the ribbon — the last color she had seen in all the world — was somewhere out there, tied to a wrist, going on ahead of her, out of reach and out of sight, but not, she swore, not ever, out of her heart.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth
set.description: Seventeen-year-old only daughter of the Earl of Ashworth; still locked in her mother's rooms at Blackwood Hall, days after the flogging. She wears the ruined white silk betrothal gown, her hair down, her mother's pearls cold at her throat; her split knuckles are healing; she has grown hollow from days without food (she refused the tray, then the Earl ordered food withheld until she cooperated; she drinks water from the ewer). She refused the seamstress's measurements for the wedding gown. For four days she refused all speech and food, standing at the window writing Callum's name on the glass in her breath and watching the empty road. On the fourth night Elsie brought her news (via Ned Tarrant and Cook) that Purvis's herring boat is gone from the cove and the oilcloth of pennies with it — Callum is believed to have escaped the county, free — which loosened the not-knowing by a thread. That same night Elsie confessed her betrayal under threat of the whip; Rosalind forgave her with a wounded, forgiving silence, telling her to bring water and not be whipped or damned, saying the men who deserve damning are not in the room. She has learned the wedding is set for the first Sunday after the harvest moon and that her father shows no mercy ('It is done. She has had her chance to be a daughter'). Emotional state: spirit drained into a grey endurance; her heart hardened into a clean, deep wound where fury should be; she has chosen endurance as the only shape her love can take, and her vow to keep loving Callum holds. She does not know if he lives or dies, only that he is gone. Location: locked room (her mother's rooms), Blackwood Hall. Goal: endure the wedding and whatever follows, keep Callum alive in her heart, watch the empty road.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: The Earl of Ashworth, cold, prideful, performing fear of Viscount Wyndham, who holds his debts. He has not visited Rosalind since locking her in. He set the wedding for the first Sunday after the harvest moon, sent the village seamstress to take her measurements (she refused), and ordered her food withheld until she cooperates — 'Let her starve a day and see how her pride fares. It is done. She has had her chance to be a daughter.' Below, the wedding preparations proceed: hammering, flowers, favors, maids' laughter, his voice giving orders, and low satisfied talk of settlements and seasons with the Viscount's people. The last of his feeling for his daughter died the night he let them take her. Location: Blackwood Hall, overseeing wedding preparations. Goal: preserve the Ashworth name by delivering Rosalind to Wyndham on the first Sunday after the harvest moon, whatever it costs her.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's lady's maid, a quiet village girl with clever hands and a careful mouth, the one who carried the full secret of the escape.
