At the flogging her weeping face gave the secret away to the Viscount's plain-coated man; two days before the ball that man found her in the kitchen passage and threatened her with the whip, and she told him the copse, the horses, and the hour, believing it would stop the lovers and let the boy live. On the fourth night after the flogging her guilt broke her: she fell to her knees in Rosalind's room and confessed everything, saying she'd rather the whip than her mistress's silence. Rosalind forgave her with a wounded, forgiving silence — told her to bring water, go, sleep, and that she would not see her whipped or damned for it. Elsie also brought the news that Callum is believed to have escaped by sea (Purvis's boat gone, the oilcloth of pennies gone). Her guilt is eased but still heavy; she will atone through service and loyalty. Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing and Rosalind's door. Goal: protect her mistress, serve her faithfully, never betray her again.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old former stable hand of Blackwood Hall, exiled after thirty strokes of the cat-o'-nine-tails, his back laid open, ribs bruised, face bloodied; he made no sound through the count and mouthed the old vow at Rosalind's window before being driven out the yard gate down the long road into the fog on pain of death. As of the fourth night after the flogging, rumored to have reached the cove: Purvis's herring boat is gone from its mooring and the oilcloth of saved pennies with it, and Ned Tarrant and Cook believe he is out of the county and free — unconfirmed, as Rosalind has not seen him and does not know if he lives. He carries the grey rag of his torn shirt and the faded blue ribbon tied around his wrist, the last color Rosalind saw before the fog closed. Location: believed fled the Blackwood lands by sea toward a coast across the water. Goal: survive the wound and the crossing, keep the ribbon and the knowing of Rosalind, never set foot on Ashworth ground again on pain of death.

In the days after the flogging Rosalind refused food and speech while locked in her mother's rooms, refused the seamstress's measurements for the wedding gown, and wrote Callum's name on the window glass in her breath. The Earl responded by ordering her food withheld until she cooperates; she grew hollow and drank only water. Her silence broke on the fourth night when she spoke to Elsie.

The Earl fixed the wedding for the first Sunday after the harvest moon, the settlements ridden with the Viscount's man, and the village seamstress summoned; below Rosalind's room the wedding preparations proceed — hammering, flowers, favors, maids' laughter. Rosalind learned this through the door and understood she will be delivered to the Viscount regardless of what she wants.

On the fourth night after the flogging Elsie brought Rosalind news from Ned Tarrant and Cook: Purvis's herring boat is gone from its mooring at the cove and the oilcloth of Callum's saved pennies with it; Callum is believed to have escaped the county, free. Unconfirmed — Rosalind has not seen him and does not know if he lives or dies, but the not-knowing loosened by a thread and she knows he is gone. This seeds the rumors of Ch. 15-18 of a thin, scarred man working docks and coastal villages across the sea.

On the fourth night Elsie broke: she confessed that two days before the ball the Viscount's plain-coated man found her in the kitchen passage, told her her weeping face had given everything away at the flogging, and threatened her with the whip unless she told when and where; she told them the copse, the horses, and the hour, believing it would stop the lovers and let the boy live. Rosalind forgave her with a wounded, forgiving silence — a clean deep wound where fury should have been — told her she would not see her whipped or damned, and bade her bring water and go. Elsie's guilt is eased but not erased.

The marriage ceremony proceeds on the first Sunday after the harvest moon at Blackwood Hall: Rosalind, hollow and silent, is dressed and delivered to Viscount Wyndham, becoming Lady Wyndham and journeying to Wyndham Hall, where the private cruelty of the first night begins (Ch. 13).

Rosalind will later hear rumors of Callum: first a thin, scarred man working the docks in a distant port town (Ch. 15), then a more detailed report of him living in a small coastal village far across the sea (Ch. 16), where he will die of a wasting grief and the blue ribbon will be returned to her (Ch. 18-19).

chapters.name: The Vow of Ashes
chapters.content:
The harvest moon rose over Blackwood Hall on the last night of the old season, fat and yellow as a coin, and Rosalind watched it from her window and thought: they have timed it to the moon. They have made even the moon their servant.

In the morning they came for her.

She heard the footsteps on the stair before dawn — many footsteps, not Elsie's alone — and she was ready, or as ready as a body can be that has been hollowed out and filled with grey. She had slept in small broken pieces, and she had washed her face in the ewer and braided her own hair, because it did not matter. Nothing about her mattered anymore except the thing they could not reach, and that was packed safe where no hand would find it.

Elsie came in first, alone, with a cup of weak tea and a face that had been crying in the dark. "Miss," she said, and stopped.

"Say it," Rosalind said. Her voice was quiet, worn smooth as sea glass. "Tell me what they have decided."

"The Viscount's man came at first light. The wedding is to be this morning, miss — before the guests, in the chapel, with only the household. They say the Viscount wants it done before the road turns." Elsie's voice cracked. "They've brought the dress."

Rosalind closed her eyes. She had refused the measurements; still they had brought a dress, and of course they had. In a house full of women who could fit a gown to a stranger's back by the look of her, there was no refusal that could not be answered with pins and patience.

"Let them bring it," she said. "I will wear it."

Elsie stared at her, and the tears spilled over, and she pressed her apron to her mouth.

"I know what you think," Rosalind said, turning from the window. Her mother's pearls lay cold on the dressing table, and she fastened them around her throat with steady hands, the way a woman fastens a collar. "It is done, Elsie. It has been done since the night he stood in the yard and counted. The only thing I can choose now is how I walk down the aisle, and I will not walk it weeping. He would not want that."

She did not say the name. They had learned, the two of them, to keep the name off their tongues in the daytime, as if the walls could hear. Perhaps they could. The house had listened to everything else.

The dress was white — of course it was white — a stiff, costly silk run up in the county town, and it fit her well enough, which was its own small cruelty, because it meant they had been looking at her all along. Elsie did the fastenings with fingers that shook, and when she was done she stood back and said, "You look —" and could not finish, because there was no word for what she looked like. A bride. A ghost in a bride's body.

They had not given her flowers. She did not ask. She walked down the back stairs on Elsie's arm because her legs had forgotten how to be strong, and the house opened around her in a hush of white — white flowers on the stair rails, white ribbons on the doors, white favors on the servants' livery — and every servant she passed looked at the floor.

The chapel was cold. Blackwood's chapel had always been cold, a narrow stone room where the Ashworths had been christened and married and buried for three hundred years. Her father stood at the altar with the Viscount's man and a priest Rosalind did not know, a thin, sallow stranger in black who looked at his book and not at her. The Viscount stood at the altar rail with his hands clasped behind his back, the same posture as the day he had stood in the drawing room and told her to walk, and his pale eyes went over her once, head to foot, and he nodded, once, as if a ledger had balanced.

Her father did not look at her. When she reached the altar he did not offer his arm; he simply stepped aside, and she understood that the last of him had gone out of the world, and what remained was a creditor presenting a debt for collection.

The priest read the service in a flat, hurrying drone. Rosalind heard the words — lawfully wedded, forsaking all others, for richer, for poorer — and they fell around her like snow on water, vanishing without a mark. She made the sounds the service required, and the Viscount's ring — heavy, cold, too large for her finger — went on her hand, and she felt it there like a shackle fitted to her exact weight.

The Viscount kissed her. It was not a kiss; it was a seal, a stamp of ownership pressed against her mouth before the priest and her father and the empty pews, dry and contemptuous and brief. When he drew back his pale eyes were satisfied, and he said, low, so only she could hear, "Lady Wyndham. I trust you will learn to like your name. You will be wearing it a long time."

She was Lady Wyndham. The words went through her and found no place to land, and she stood in the cold chapel with her mother's pearls at her throat and thought: I am no more his than I was my father's. I was never theirs. I was his, only his, and he is gone, and they may name me anything they like.

There was a small cold breakfast that no one ate, and then the carriage was brought around, the black carriage with the four exhausted horses, and Elsie came down the steps with Rosalind's small trunk and stood at the bottom looking up at her.

"The ribbons," Elsie said, low, so only Rosalind heard. "The white ones on the doors. I took them down this morning and burned them. It seemed wrong to leave them up."

"Thank you," Rosalind said. "That is the kindest thing anyone has done for me in a year."

She did not look back at Blackwood Hall as the carriage drew away. She did not look at her father standing in the doorway. She looked straight ahead through the carriage glass at the grey moor sliding past, and she felt the miles open between her and everything she had ever known, and she did not weep, because weeping was a thing the living did, and she was no longer sure she was among them.

The journey took two days. They stopped the first night at an inn in the town where the roads crossed, and the Viscount drank and played cards with his man and did not speak to her except to tell her to eat, which she could not. She sat in the corner of the private room with her cold hands folded in her lap and watched him, and she learned the shape of the thing she had married the way you learn the shape of a room in the dark: by the edges of it. He had a way of looking at the innkeeper's daughter that made the girl leave in a hurry. He had a way of finishing a sentence and looking at her as if daring her to speak, and she did not speak, and something in his eyes flickered, and she understood that her silence was a small disobedience, and that he had noted it, and that he would collect it.

On the second day the road climbed out of the low country into the high moors, and the sea appeared at the edge of the world, grey and endless, and she thought of a herring boat and a boy with a scarred back and a blue ribbon around his wrist, and pressed her hand to the glass and felt nothing.

Wyndham Hall stood above the sea at the end of a long avenue of wind-bent trees, a great black house of stone built to outlast everything, and it did. It was larger than Blackwood — larger than any house she had ever seen — and it was silent. No children ran in the yard. No dogs barked. The servants who came out to take the horses moved like shadows and did not look at her, and she understood that they had been trained the way the Viscount trained his horses, and that she was now under the same hand.

The Viscount's mother was waiting in the great hall. She was a tall, straight-backed woman in black, with her son's pale eyes and a face that had been emptied of feeling so long ago that the emptiness had become the shape of her, and she looked at Rosalind the way one looks at a new piece of furniture delivered slightly damaged.

"This is the Ashworth girl," she said. It was not a question.

"She is Lady Wyndham now," the Viscount said, "and she will answer to it. Mother, show her the house. I have business."

He was gone without another word, and the old woman stood with her pale eyes on Rosalind and said, "You will find the house is kept quiet. My son does not care for noise. You will find the servants are kept quiet; my son does not care for gossip. You will find, in time, that you are kept quiet too." She turned and walked down the corridor, and Rosalind followed, because there was nowhere else to go.

They gave her a room at the top of the great staircase, a high cold room with a four-poster bed and windows that looked out over the sea — the Viscount's mother's choice, meant to impress and isolate. The bed was hung with damask the color of dried blood. The windows were barred. The sea beyond them was grey, and the sky was grey, and the moors that sloped down to the cliffs were grey, and she stood at the window and watched the waves break on the rocks far below and thought: so this is the shape of it. The hayloft was the only real thing I ever had, and they took it, and this grey, silent, beautiful prison was what they had been building for me the whole time.

She did not unpack. She sat on the edge of the bed in her traveling dress and waited. Below her the house settled into its evening silence, and the sea went on with its grey work, and the footsteps came up the stairs.

The Viscount came into the room without knocking. He had shed his coat and his cravat, and he stood in his shirtsleeves in the doorway looking at her, and she saw the satisfaction settle on his face like a man coming home to a room he has been promised.

"So," he said, closing the door behind him. "Here we are."

She stood. She had not planned to stand; her body did it without her. He crossed the room and reached out and took her chin in his hand — not gently, not roughly, just held it, turning her face to the light — and looked at her the way he had looked at her in the drawing room at Blackwood, adding up her parts.

"You're thinner than I ordered," he said. "I told your father I don't care for the fashion of starving women. I don't care for men who fail to follow orders." His thumb pressed into the hinge of her jaw, hard enough that she felt it in her teeth. "But we'll mend that. I am very patient with my property."

She did not answer. There was nothing to answer; he had not asked a question. But her silence made something in his pale eyes go flat and cold, and his grip on her chin tightened, and she felt the bruise beginning to form under his fingers like a flower opening.

"When I speak to you," he said, "you will answer."

She looked at him. She looked into his pale, empty eyes, and she thought of a lantern burning in a hayloft, and warm scarred hands, and a voice that said we carry it together, or not at all — and she found that she could look at this man and feel nothing at all, because the thing he wanted to break was not in the room with him. It was out on the grey sea, tied to a wrist, going on ahead of her.

"Yes, my lord," she said.

The word came out flat and dead, and he heard the flatness, and his grip tightened again until the pain was a bright thing, and then he let go with a contemptuous shove that sent her stumbling back against the bedpost. She felt the wood drive into her spine and made no sound.

"There," he said, pleased. "That is the first lesson. You will learn the rest in time. I am told you are clever, and I believe cleverness can be taught out of a woman if the lessons are firm enough." He smiled, a small, tight, knowing smile, the smile of a man who has just closed a door on something that will never get out. "Welcome to Wyndham Hall, Lady Wyndham. You will find it is a very long house, and a very long life, and you will spend all of it learning to obey me."

He turned and left, and the door closed, and the key turned in the lock — a small bright sound in the silence — and Rosalind stood alone in the high cold room above the grey sea with the bruise flowering on her jaw, and she pressed her hand to the place over her heart where the ribbon would have been if she still had it, and she whispered to the empty room:

"I will not stop loving him. Whatever you do to me. I will not stop."

She said it to the sea. She said it to the barred window and the damask bed and the key in the lock. She said it to the boy who was somewhere out on the water with a scarred back and a blue ribbon around his wrist, and she made a vow in the ashes of everything they had taken from her: she would endure. She would wear his name like a collar and learn his lessons and smile with dead eyes — and somewhere underneath it all, in the place no hand could reach, she would keep the boy alive, and the vow alive, and the love alive, the only thing they had not been able to take, the only thing they would never take, as long as there was breath in her body.

The sea went grey below the window. The house went silent around her. And in the high cold room, the new Lady Wyndham stood very still, with a bruise on her jaw and a wedding ring cold on her finger and a heart that beat, and beat, and beat, against the bars of the world, refusing to stop.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: Stood apart at the wedding like a creditor presenting a debt for collection; did not look at her, did not offer his arm, said nothing as the black carriage carried her away; stood in the doorway watching it go. The last of his feeling for his daughter is dead; his debts are settled by the Viscount's gold and his name is saved. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: his obligations discharged; he has spent his daughter and is done.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Dressed Rosalind in the white silk for the wedding with shaking fingers, unable to finish the sentence 'You look —'. Before the carriage left she told Rosalind she had taken down the white wedding ribbons from the doors and burned them because it seemed wrong to leave them up; Rosalind called it the kindest thing done for her in a year. She watched the black carriage carry her mistress away, then remained at Blackwood Hall with her guilt eased but not erased. She does not know what will become of Rosalind at Wyndham Hall. Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing. Goal: serve and atone; keep whatever watch she can from afar.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old exiled stable hand, back scarred from thirty strokes, believed to have escaped by sea on Purvis's herring boat with the oilcloth of saved pennies; unconfirmed — Rosalind does not know if he lives. He carries the faded blue ribbon tied around his wrist, the last color she saw before the fog closed. As Rosalind traveled to Wyndham Hall she pictured him somewhere out on the grey water with a scarred back and the ribbon. Location: unknown, believed fled the Blackwood lands across the sea. Goal: survive the wound and the crossing, keep the ribbon and the knowing of Rosalind, never set foot on Ashworth ground again on pain of death.

set.name: Rosalind Ashworth (Lady Wyndham)
set.description: Now Rosalind Wyndham, née Ashworth, married that morning at Blackwood Hall before the harvest-moon Sunday guests (a small household ceremony; the Viscount wanted it done before the road turned). She wore a white silk gown she never measured, her mother's pearls, and the Viscount's heavy cold ring; the priest was a stranger, her father stood apart like a creditor presenting a debt, and the Viscount's sealing kiss was dry and contemptuous. She did not look back at Blackwood as the carriage left; Elsie had burned the white door ribbons and told her, and Rosalind called it the kindest thing done for her in a year. Journey of two days: first night at an inn where the Viscount ignored her and noted her silence as a small disobedience to be collected; on the second day the road climbed to the high moors and she saw the grey sea and thought of Callum and the boat. Arrived at Wyndham Hall, a great black silent house above the sea at the end of an avenue of wind-bent trees; met the Viscount's mother, a tall straight-backed woman with the Viscount's pale eyes who warned her the house, servants, and she herself will be kept quiet. Given a high cold room with barred windows over the grey sea, a four-poster bed hung with blood-red damask. That night the Viscount came to her room: took her chin, pressed a bruise into her jaw, demanded she answer when spoken to, shoved her against the bedpost, and delivered the first lesson in obedience — 'welcome to Wyndham Hall... you will spend all of it learning to obey me' — then locked her in. Emotional state: hollow endurance; she looked into his pale eyes and felt nothing because the thing he wants to break is not in the room — her love for Callum lives somewhere no hand can reach. She has sworn a vow of ashes: to endure, wear his name like a collar, learn his lessons, smile with dead eyes, and keep the boy, the vow, and the love alive underneath. Physical condition: thinner from the days of withheld food, bruise flowering on her jaw, wedding ring cold on her finger. Location: locked high room, Wyndham Hall, above the grey sea. Goal: endure whatever follows, keep Callum alive in her heart, survive.

set.name: Viscount Marcus Wyndham
set.description: Married Rosalind that morning at Blackwood Hall in a cold ceremony he timed before the road turned. Sealed the marriage with a dry contemptuous kiss, called her Lady Wyndham, and told her she will be wearing the name a long time. Traveled two days with her without speaking beyond ordering her to eat; noted her flat silence as a small disobedience to be collected. At Wyndham Hall he left the house to his mother's keeping and went to his business, then that night came to her room in his shirtsleeves: gripped her chin, pressed a bruise into her jaw, demanded she answer when spoken to, shoved her against the bedpost, and delivered the first lesson in obedience — 'cleverness can be taught out of a woman if the lessons are firm enough' — before locking her in. He trains servants, horses, and women with the same firm hand; he is patient with his property. Location: Wyndham Hall, above the sea. Goal: break her will through patient lessons and own her completely.

set.name: The Dowager Lady Wyndham (the Viscount's mother)
set.description: A tall, straight-backed woman in black with her son's pale eyes and a face emptied of feeling long ago. Met Rosalind in the great hall, calling her 'the Ashworth girl,' and warned her that the house is kept quiet, the servants are kept quiet, and in time she will be kept quiet too. She chose Rosalind's high cold room with barred windows over the sea — meant to impress and isolate. She lives at Wyndham Hall, a mirror of her son's cruelty, reduced to emptiness. Goal: maintain the house's silence and order.

The marriage ceremony took place the morning after the harvest moon at Blackwood Hall's cold chapel before a stranger priest, the Viscount's man, and only the household — the Viscount wanted it done before the road turned. Rosalind wore a white silk gown she had never measured (they had been looking at her all along), her mother's pearls, and the Viscount's heavy ring. Her father stood apart like a creditor presenting a debt; the Viscount's sealing kiss was dry and contemptuous, and he told her she will wear the name Lady Wyndham a long time. She is now legally the Viscount's wife.

After the wedding a two-day journey in the black carriage with four exhausted horses: the first night at an inn where the Viscount drank and played cards, ordered her to eat, and noted her flat silence as a small disobedience to be collected; the second day the road climbed into the high moors and the grey sea appeared, and she pressed her hand to the glass thinking of Callum's boat. Wyndham Hall is a great black silent house above the sea at the end of an avenue of wind-bent trees, larger than Blackwood, servants trained like horses who move like shadows. The Viscount's mother met her in the great hall and warned her everything will be kept quiet.

Before the carriage left, Elsie told Rosalind she had taken down the white wedding ribbons from the doors and burned them because it seemed wrong to leave them up. Rosalind called it the kindest thing anyone had done for her in a year. The ribbons are gone.

On the first night at Wyndham Hall the Viscount came to Rosalind's room in his shirtsleeves and delivered the first lesson in obedience: he took her chin, pressed a bruise into her jaw, demanded she answer when spoken to, shoved her against the bedpost, and told her cleverness can be taught out of a woman if the lessons are firm enough, and that she will spend a very long life learning to obey him — then locked her in. Rosalind felt nothing looking at him because the love he wants to break is not in the room; she whispered her vow to the empty room and swore to endure, wearing his name like a collar, keeping the boy alive underneath. Her suffering has only begun.

Life at Wyndham Hall unfolds in methodical cruelty: the Viscount humiliates her in company, isolates her from potential friends, and takes pleasure in her misery; she learns to smile with dead eyes while her heart rots (Ch. 14). Her locked-in, isolated state in the high barred room is the seed of this grey imprisonment.

The Dowager Lady Wyndham's warning that the house, the servants, and Rosalind herself will be kept quiet establishes the silence that will isolate Rosalind at Wyndham Hall across the grey years — no letters answered, no friends made (Ch. 14, 17).

chapters.name: The Gilded Prison
chapters.content:
The key turned in the lock every night, and every morning it turned again, and within a week Rosalind had learned to measure her life by that small bright sound the way the house measured its days by the tide. Morning: the key, the door, the tray. Evening: the key, the door, the Viscount. The sea between the bars did its grey work below, and the high cold room above it filled with the particular silence of a place where nothing is allowed to happen.

The bruise on her jaw faded from purple to yellow to nothing, and she thought, on the day it was gone: he will make another. It was not prophecy. It was arithmetic. She had begun to understand her new husband the way she had once understood the seasons — by their returns.

They let her out for dinner. That was the shape of it: the Viscount came for her himself at seven, or sent his mother, and she walked down the great staircase in whatever gown they had laid out, and sat at the long table, and was a wife. On the first night there were no guests, and the two of them ate in a silence the servants moved through like fish through water, and the Viscount watched her over the candles with the patience of a man reading a book he intends to finish.

"You will answer when spoken to," he said at the second course, and she said, "Yes, my lord," and he nodded, once, satisfied, as if a dog had sat when told.

She learned the rules the way a prisoner learns the walls — by walking into them. Answer when spoken to. Do not begin speech. Do not look at the footmen. Do not let your eyes rest on anything he has not given you. Eat what is set before you. Be seen, and not heard, and above all be calm, because a calm wife is a wife who has learned, and a wife who has learned is a wife he will grow bored of, and boredom was the only mercy she could imagine.

The cruelty was methodical. She had expected a storm; she had not expected weather. He did not strike her often. He did not need to. He had discovered early that her face gave her away — that a certain remark about servants, about runaways, about the price of herring and the men who worked the coast, could make something move behind her eyes — and so he said those things, and watched for the movement, and when he found it his pale eyes warmed with a slow, private pleasure, like a man turning a coin over to admire the die.

"My wife," he said at the first dinner with guests — county neighbours, a Sir and a Lady and their hollow-eyed daughter — "does not care for the sea. She finds it grey. I find it honest. It keeps what it is given and gives back only what it must." His hand lay on the table beside hers, and he smiled at her, and the guests smiled, uncertain, and Rosalind smiled with her mouth and kept her eyes dead, and beneath the cloth his hand found her wrist and held it, not hard, just held it, the way you hold a horse you are not sure of.

"Play for us," he said later, in the drawing room, and it was not a request, and she sat at the instrument they had wheeled in for the purpose and played the piece her governess had beaten into her at thirteen, her fingers going through it without her, and when she finished he said, "There. You see. She learns quickly," and the guests applauded the way one applauds a trick.

She learned to smile with dead eyes. That was the true art of Wyndham Hall, and the Dowager was its mistress. The old woman watched her from the corners of rooms, from the landings of stairs, from the high window of the morning room where she sat with needlework that was never finished, and Rosalind understood that she was being studied — her silences, her sighs, her hands — the way a groom studies a new horse for vices. In company the Dowager called her "Lady Wyndham" with exact politeness and introduced her to no one, so that she stood at the edge of every room like furniture, and when Rosalind tried, once, to speak to the hollow-eyed daughter, the girl looked at the Dowager first, and the Dowager's pale eyes moved, and the girl found she had urgent business elsewhere.

That was the isolation, and it was done without a word of prohibition. She was allowed to write letters. That was the cruellest mercy, because the letters went nowhere.

At night, when the key had turned and the house had settled into its silence, she wrote to Callum. She had no address, so she wrote to the sea. She wrote on the backs of household bills and the blank leaves of the music books, in a small cramped hand, the things she could not say in the daytime where the walls listened. I am learning to be a wife, she wrote. I am learning to be nothing. I believe you are alive because I have decided it, and I will not be argued with by the grey water. She wrote that she had worn his name inside her name all day. She wrote that she had seen a herring boat from the barred window and stood at the glass until it was a speck, and that she had imagined him on it, whole, scarred, alive, with the blue ribbon around his wrist. She wrote the word hayloft and stopped, because the word undid her, and she sat with the pen shaking until she could go on. And when the letter was finished — as long as she could bear — she folded it small, knelt at the grate, and burned it, and watched his name turn to ash, and told herself the smoke went up and out, past the bars, over the sea, to wherever he was.

She wrote to Blackwood Hall too. To her father, formally, the first time — a short, correct letter asking after the health of the house, the horses, her maid. She did not ask to come home. There was no home. She asked only for word, any word, the way a woman in a well asks for rope. The answer came back six weeks later, in her father's own hand, unopened: the Ashworth seal intact across the flap, the address crossed out. A message without words: you are no longer mine to answer.

She wrote to Elsie. That letter she did not burn; she sealed it and gave it to a footman, and the footman gave it to the Dowager, and the Dowager burned it in the morning room with the same economy with which she burned the household accounts. Rosalind never knew. She only knew that she wrote and wrote into the silence, and the silence wrote nothing back, and after a year she stopped writing to Blackwood and kept only the letters to the sea, which needed no answer and promised none.

The grey years began. That was how she came to think of them, not as days but as weather — a long slow weather that had settled over Wyndham Hall and did not intend to lift. The Derwents' autumn ball at Merriwether House came and went without her, her father having cried off on the pretext of the wedding, and the blue gown Mrs. Haversham had made hung in a press at Blackwood, unworn, and Rosalind did not think of it. Autumn bled into winter; winter into a spring that came late and went early; the sea stayed grey through all of it. The Viscount went about his business — his rides, his ledgers, his long absences in the county town — and the house went on in its silence, and the Dowager's needlework was never finished, and Rosalind moved through the days like a ghost who had forgotten how to frighten anyone.

The cruelty did not relent, because it was not a passion but a schedule — a thing he did on Tuesdays and Thursdays and whenever the mood took him, as regular as the tide. He took pleasure in her misery. She had known it from the first lesson, but she learned its full shape in the years: the way he would wait for the one remark that found the crack in her calm, and then stay on it, working it, the way a man works a splinter out of a thumb — slowly, with satisfaction, drawing the pain up to the surface where he could see it. And she learned to deny him. That was her skill now, her only skill: the dead smile, the flat eyes, the voice that answered, "Yes, my lord," and gave him nothing back. When he hurt her she made her face a wall, and she watched his pleasure dim, and she counted it a victory though she bled for it.

In the nights she kept her vigil. The sea glass he had given her lived in the hem of her oldest gown, where no hand but hers would find it, and she held it in the dark and made it warm. She rehearsed him the way the Dowager rehearsed her needlework — stitch by stitch, until the pattern was perfect and could not be lost: his voice, his hands, the lantern burning, the smell of hay and horses, the way he had said her name the first time, low, as if it cost him something. She did not know if he lived. The not-knowing was a wound she had learned to carry, and on her worst nights she told herself that no wound is proof of death — that the sea keeps what it is given but gives back only what it must, and that the boy who had taught himself to want was too stubborn to stop wanting.

She wrote his name on the window glass in her breath, the way she had done at Blackwood, and watched it fade, and wrote it again.

"Whatever you do to me," she whispered to the locked room, to the barred window, to the grey sea, "I will not stop. I will not stop."

The years went grey. The house went silent. And in the high cold room above the sea, the Lady Wyndham they had made knelt at her grate and burned her letters and held her sea glass and kept, underneath the dead eyes and the careful smile, the only thing they had never been able to reach: the boy, and the vow, and the love that was never permitted to live — alive, and waiting, and refusing to die.

set.name: Earl Ashworth (Rosalind's father)
set.description: At Blackwood Hall, his debts settled by the Viscount's gold, his name saved, the last of his feeling for his daughter dead. When Rosalind wrote him once during the first grey years, formally asking after the health of the house, the horses, and her maid, his answer came back six weeks later unopened — the Ashworth seal intact, the address crossed out: a wordless message that she is no longer his to answer. He cried off the Derwents' autumn ball on the pretext of the wedding, so the blue gown Mrs. Haversham made hangs unworn in a press. Location: Blackwood Hall. Goal: his obligations discharged; he has spent his daughter and is done.

set.name: Elsie
set.description: Rosalind's former lady's maid at Blackwood Hall, still in service there with her guilt eased but not erased. She does not know that Rosalind wrote her a letter during the first grey years, or that the Dowager burned it with the household accounts; from her side she has kept whatever watch she can from afar, and heard nothing from Wyndham Hall. Location: Blackwood Hall, servants' wing. Goal: serve and atone; keep whatever watch she can from afar.

set.name: Callum (the stable hand)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old exiled stable hand, back scarred from thirty strokes, believed to have escaped by sea on Purvis's herring boat with the oilcloth of saved pennies — unconfirmed. Across the grey years Rosalind does not know if he lives or dies; she has decided he is alive and refuses to be argued with by the grey water. She imagines him on herring boats, whole, scarred, alive, with the faded blue ribbon around his wrist. He carries the ribbon tied around his wrist, the last color she saw before the fog closed, and the knowing of Rosalind. Location: unknown, believed fled the Blackwood lands across the sea; working some coast where a scarred back and a ribbon are his only goods. Goal: survive, keep the ribbon and the knowing of Rosalind, never set foot on Ashworth ground again on pain of death.

set.name: Viscount Marcus Wyndham
set.description: Rosalind's husband, master of Wyndham Hall. Across the first grey years his cruelty has become methodical — a schedule, not a passion, as regular as the tide: he does not strike her often but finds the remark that moves something behind her dead eyes (servants, runaways, the price of herring, men who work the coast) and works it slowly with satisfaction. He lets her out for dinner at seven (or sends his mother), watches her across the candles with the patience of a man reading a book he intends to finish, and is pleased when she answers on command ('Yes, my lord'). He humiliates her in company: at the first dinner with county neighbours he told the guests she finds the sea grey, held her wrist under the cloth, then commanded her to play piano as a trick. He takes pleasure in her misery and is frustrated by her flat dead-eyed calm, which he reads as a small continuing disobedience to be worked out of her. He trains servants, horses, and women with the same firm hand and is patient with his property. Location: Wyndham Hall, above the sea. Goal: break her will through patient, methodical lessons and own her completely.

set.name: The Dowager Lady Wyndham (the Viscount's mother)
set.description: The Viscount's mother, a tall straight-backed woman in black with her son's pale eyes. She has become the house's instrument of isolation: she studies Rosalind from corners, landings, and the morning-room window like a groom studying a new horse for vices, introduces her to no one in company (so Rosalind stands at the edge of rooms like furniture), and wordlessly drove away the hollow-eyed daughter the moment Rosalind tried to befriend her. She intercepts Rosalind's letters — she burned the letter to Elsie with the household accounts; Rosalind never knew. She sits with needlework that is never finished, the mirror of her son's cruelty, reduced to emptiness. Location: Wyndham Hall. Goal: maintain the house's silence and order; keep Rosalind isolated and quiet.

set.name: Rosalind Wyndham (née Ashworth)
set.description: Lady Wyndham, married to Viscount Marcus Wyndham, ~18, living at Wyndham Hall above the grey sea. The first grey years have begun. Locked in her high cold room with barred windows over the sea each night (key turned in the lock at night, morning, and before dinner), she has learned to measure her life by that small bright sound and by the tide. The bruise on her jaw faded and healed; she expects him to make another. She has learned the house's rules by walking into them: answer when spoken to, never begin speech, don't look at footmen, don't rest her eyes on anything not given her, eat what is set, be calm. His cruelty is methodical — not storms but weather: he does not strike often, but he finds the remark that moves something behind her eyes (servants, runaways, the price of herring, men who work the coast) and works it slowly like a splinter, taking private pleasure in her misery, on a schedule as regular as the tide. She has learned to smile with dead eyes and deny him her pain — her only skill — and counts it a victory though she bleeds. She plays piano for guests as a trick; at the first dinner with county neighbours (a Sir, a Lady, a hollow-eyed daughter) he held her wrist under the cloth and later made her play. The Dowager studies her from corners and introduced her to no one; when she tried to speak to the hollow-eyed daughter, the girl looked to the Dowager and fled. Isolation is enforced wordlessly. She writes letters to Callum at night on the backs of bills and blank music leaves — with no address she writes to the sea, telling him she is learning to be nothing, that she believes he is alive because she has decided it, describing the herring boat seen from the barred window — and burns each one at the grate, watching his name turn to ash and telling herself the smoke goes over the sea to him. She wrote to her father once (formal, asking after the house, horses, her maid); six weeks later his answer came back unopened, seal intact, address crossed out — a wordless message that she is no longer his to answer. She wrote to Elsie, gave it to a footman; the Dowager burned it with the household accounts and Rosalind never knew. After a year she stopped writing to Blackwood and kept only the sea letters. The Derwents' autumn ball at Merriwether House came and went without her; her father cried off on pretext of the wedding and the blue gown hangs unworn in a press at Blackwood. She keeps the sea glass Callum gave her sewn in the hem of her oldest gown, warms it in her hands in the dark, and rehearses him stitch by stitch — his voice, his hands, the lantern, the smell of hay, the way he said her name — to keep the pattern perfect and unlosable. She writes his name on the window glass in her breath as at Blackwood. Emotional state: dead-eyed endurance; a grey patience; the not-knowing of whether he lives is a wound she has learned to carry; her vow holds — she will not stop loving him, whatever is done to her. Physical condition: thinner, muted, alive; the sea glass is her hidden relic. Location: locked high room, Wyndham Hall, above the grey sea. Goal: endure the grey years, deny the Viscount her pain, keep Callum and the vow alive underneath, survive.

During the first grey years at Wyndham Hall Rosalind learned the house's rules the way a prisoner learns walls — by walking into them: answer when spoken to, never begin speech, do not look at the footmen, do not rest her eyes on anything not given her, eat what is set, be seen and not heard, be calm. The key turns in the lock nightly, mornings, and before dinner; she measures her life by that small bright sound and by the tide. The cruelty is methodical, a schedule as regular as the tide: the Viscount finds the remark that moves something behind her eyes (servants, runaways, the price of herring, men who work the coast) and works it slowly with satisfaction.

At the first dinner with county neighbours (a Sir, a Lady, and a hollow-eyed daughter), the Viscount announced Rosalind 'does not care for the sea. She finds it grey,' held her wrist under the cloth while the guests smiled uncertainly, then commanded her to play piano as a trick in the drawing room; the guests applauded the way one applauds a trick. The Dowager introduced her to no one and wordlessly drove off the hollow-eyed daughter the moment Rosalind tried to befriend her — the isolation is enforced without a word of prohibition.

Across the first grey years, at night after the key turned, Rosalind wrote letters to Callum on the backs of household bills and the blank leaves of music books in a small cramped hand — with no address she wrote to the sea: 'I am learning to be a wife. I am learning to be nothing,' that she believes he is alive because she has decided it, that she saw a herring boat from the barred window and imagined him on it, whole, scarred, alive, with the blue ribbon around his wrist — and burned each one at the grate, watching his name turn to ash, telling herself the smoke goes over the sea to him.

Rosalind wrote once to her father at Blackwood Hall, formally asking after the health of the house, the horses, and her maid. Six weeks later the answer came back unopened — the Ashworth seal intact across the flap, the address crossed out: a wordless message that she is no longer his to answer. After a year she stopped writing to Blackwood and kept only the letters to the sea.

Rosalind wrote a letter to Elsie and gave it to a footman; the footman gave it to the Dowager, who burned it in the morning room with the same economy with which she burned the household accounts. Rosalind never knew; she only knew she wrote into a silence that wrote nothing back.

The Derwents' autumn ball at Merriwether House came and went during the first grey years without Rosalind: her father cried off on the pretext of the wedding, and the blue gown Mrs. Haversham made hangs unworn in a press at Blackwood Hall. (Resolves the old scheduled social obligation of future_requirement 'derwent_autumn_ball_occurs'.)

In the nights of the grey years Rosalind kept the sea glass Callum gave her sewn in the hem of her oldest gown, where no hand but hers would find it, warmed it in the dark, and rehearsed him stitch by stitch — his voice, his hands, the lantern, the smell of hay and horses, the way he said her name the first time — to keep the pattern perfect and unlosable. She writes his name on the window glass in her breath, as at Blackwood, and whispers that she will not stop loving him whatever is done to her.

During the grey years at Wyndham Hall Rosalind will hear a rumor that Callum was seen in a distant port town, thin and scarred, working the docks (Ch. 15) — the first thread of the reports that will lead to the coastal village and the ribbon's return (Ch. 16, 18-19).

Rosalind's letter to Blackwood was returned unopened by her father's hand, and her letter to Elsie was burned by the Dowager; across the grey years every inquiry she sends to Blackwood Hall is met with silence (Ch. 14, 17). No word from home will ever reach her at Wyndham Hall.

chapters.name: The Grey Years
chapters.content:
The grey years passed the way weather passes — not in days she could count but in seasons she could not stop, a long slow tide that went out and came in and went out again and never once showed her the bottom of the sea. Autumn bled into winter; winter into a spring that came late and went early; the sea stayed grey through all of it, and the high cold room above it stayed grey too, and Rosalind moved through both like a woman walking the bottom of a river, learning to breathe the water.

She did not count the years. She counted other things: the turns of the key, the comings and goings of the tide, the days between the Viscount's cruelties, which were never long. She counted the herring boats that crossed the strip of water below her barred window, and she gave each one a name, and she watched until it was a speck, and she told herself that one of them, someday, would be him. She had decided, early, that he was alive, and she would not be argued with by the grey water. It was not hope, precisely. Hope was a thing with wings, and this was a thing with hands — a stubborn, chapped, scarred-back thing that got up every morning with her and went to bed every night without her and refused, on principle, to die.

She knew nothing of his life. She imagined it instead, and her imagination was her only freedom, so she fed it carefully, the way she had once fed the little fire in the grate with her letters. She imagined him in a port town — a town of tarred ropes and tall masts and gulls crying over fish-gutted quays — because the rumour, when it came, placed him there, and she built the whole of her grey world around that one scrap of news.

The rumour came in the third grey year, or the fourth — she had stopped being sure. It came the way everything came to her at Wyndham Hall: sideways, through a door left ajar, through a servant who did not know she was listening. The Viscount had men who came up from the coast, hard weathered men who stood in the yard with their hats in their hands and spoke to him of cargo and prices and the state of the roads. One such day Rosalind stood in the upper corridor, out of sight behind the landing curtain — a small rebellion she permitted herself, to stand and listen where she was not meant to be — and heard one of the men say that down at the port, on the far side of the water, there was a fellow working the docks, a thin scarred fellow with a back like a map of welts, and that he worked like a man with nothing left to lose and talked to no one, and that he wore, tied around his wrist under the sleeve, a scrap of faded blue.

Rosalind heard it through the wall the way a prisoner hears rain, and she stood so still behind the curtain that her heart, beating, seemed loud enough to give her away. She did not move. She did not breathe. She waited for the man to say more — the name, the town, the colour of his eyes — but the men had moved on to cargo, and the word blue hung in the air like a struck bell, and she carried it back up the stairs with her, carefully, the way she carried the sea glass in her hem, and locked herself in her room and sat on the edge of the bed with her hands folded and let herself have it.

Thin, she thought. Scarred. The words were terrible and they were beautiful, and she turned them over and over like a woman counting coins she could not spend. He was thin — of course he was thin, he had always been thin, she remembered the hollow of his collarbone in the lantern light. He was scarred — she remembered the cat, the thirty strokes, the way his shirt had come away in the torchlight, and she pressed her fist against her mouth until the memory passed. He talked to no one. He worked like a man with nothing left to lose. And he wore, tied around his wrist, a scrap of faded blue.

She did not know if it was him. She would never know. The rumour could have been any man on any coast; the sea kept what it was given and gave back only what it must, and it had given her nothing but this — a story told by a hard weathered man to a hard weathered master, overheard by a wife who was not supposed to be listening. It could have been nothing. It could have been everything. And that was the cruelty of it, and the mercy of it: she could not prove it, and so she could not lose it.

She clung to the scrap of hope the way a drowning woman clings to a spar, with her whole body, with the strength that comes from knowing there is nothing else in all that grey water. It was not rational. She knew it was not rational. She had learned arithmetic in the schoolroom and she had learned the arithmetic of this house since, and the arithmetic said that a thin scarred dockworker on a far coast was more likely a stranger than a boy she had known for one spring. But the blue ribbon — she could not let the blue ribbon go. It had been hers once, her mother's, a small bright thing she had dropped in a stable yard and watched a stable boy pick up with trembling hands. If it was true that a man wore it on his wrist under his sleeve, then the boy had kept his promise: he had carried it into exile, and he was alive, and he had not stopped wanting.

She said his name to the locked room, to the barred window, to the grey sea, the way she had said it at Blackwood: Callum. And the word went out over the water, and she told herself it found him, the way she told herself the smoke of her burned letters found him, and she held the sea glass in her hand and made it warm and kept her vigil.

The Viscount's cruelty did not relent. It had never relented, and it would not relent now; it was a schedule, not a storm, as regular as the tide that worked the shore below. He had learned her rules by now — she had learned his, and he had learned hers, and the two of them circled each other across the candlelit table like two animals who knew each other's teeth. He still found the remark that moved something behind her dead eyes. He was patient, and he was clever, and he knew her the way a man knows the horse he has bought: he knew that herring made her flinch, and runaways, and the men who worked the coast, and he used them the way a surgeon uses a lancet, opening the same wound in the same place, watching for the blood.

The difference, in the grey years, was that she had begun to bleed less. Or rather — she had begun to hide the bleeding better. She had learned that survival was itself a kind of rebellion, the only kind left to her in a world that had taken everything else. When he hurt her, she made her face a wall. When he humiliated her in company — and he did, still, with his small precise cruelties, his hand on her wrist beneath the cloth, his trick with the piano, his remarks that the guests laughed at uncertainly — she smiled with her mouth and kept her eyes dead and gave him nothing, and she counted it a victory though she bled for it. They could take her name, her freedom, her future. They could lock the door and hold the key. But they could not make her feel it. That was the one thing they had never been able to reach, and she guarded it the way she guarded the sea glass in her hem, the way she guarded the rumour in her chest: fiercely, in the dark, where no one could see.

The Dowager still watched her from the corners of rooms, still sat with her needlework that was never finished, still studied her the way a groom studies a horse for vices. The old woman had grown greyer, and thinner, and her pale eyes had sunk deeper into her skull, but she did not relent either, and Rosalind understood that she would outlive them all, the Dowager and the Viscount and the house itself, if only by refusing to die of them. That was the shape of her survival now: a quiet defiance, so quiet no one heard it, so quiet it looked like submission to everyone who watched. Let them think she was broken. Let them think the lessons had taken. Underneath the dead eyes and the careful smile, under the collar of his name, she kept the boy, and the vow, and the love that was never permitted to live — and she kept them alive, and waiting, and refusing to die.

In the nights she wrote her letters to the sea, as she had always done, on the backs of bills and the blank leaves of music books, in her small cramped hand. She wrote to him about the rumour. She wrote: A man said there is a fellow at the port, thin and scarred, who talks to no one, who works like a man with nothing left to lose, who wears a scrap of faded blue around his wrist. I have decided it is you. I know it is probably not you. I have decided it anyway, and I will not be argued with, not by arithmetic, not by the grey water, not by anyone. She wrote that she was learning to be nothing, and that being nothing was a kind of armour, and that under the armour he was safe. She wrote the word hayloft, and stopped, and sat with the pen shaking, and went on. And when the letter was finished she folded it small, knelt at the grate, and burned it, and watched the words turn to ash — and told herself, as she always told herself, that the smoke went up and out, past the bars, over the sea, to wherever he was, to the thin scarred man with the blue ribbon, to the boy who had taught himself to want and had wanted her.

On the worst nights she did not write. On the worst nights she sat at the window with the sea glass in her hand and rehearsed him stitch by stitch, the way the Dowager rehearsed her needlework — his voice, his hands, the lantern burning, the smell of hay and horses, the way he had said her name the first time, low, as if it cost him something. She could not lose the pattern. She would not lose the pattern. As long as she could say his name on the glass in her breath and watch it fade and say it again, as long as she could warm the sea glass against her heart, as long as she could hold the rumour like a coin in her pocket and spend it slowly, she was not nothing. She was the woman who loved him. That was the whole of her, and it was enough, and it was everything.

The grey years passed. The sea went out and came in. The key turned in the lock morning and night, and the Viscount went about his business, and the Dowager's needlework was never finished, and Rosalind moved through the house like a ghost who had forgotten how to frighten anyone — and in the high cold room above the sea, in the dark, she kept her vigil, and she burned her letters, and she held her sea glass, and she refused to die. The world had tried to break her. It had taken her father, her name, her freedom, the boy she loved. It had beaten him bloody in a torchlit yard and driven him down a road into the fog, and it had married her to a man whose pale eyes watched her the way a man watches a horse he intends to break, and it had wrapped her in grey until she could not remember the colour of spring. And still, underneath, she kept the one thing they had never been able to reach — the love, and the vow, and the hope that was not a thing with wings but a thing with hands, a stubborn chapped scarred-back thing that refused to let go of a scrap of faded blue.

She did not know if the rumour was true. She would never know. But she had decided it was true, and she would not be argued with by the grey water — and as long as she held the knowing of him, as long as she kept the pattern perfect and unlosable, the grey years could not touch the only thing that mattered. They had not broken her. They had not broken him — she had decided that too, and she held it the way she held the sea glass, warming it in the dark. Somewhere across the water there was a thin scarred man working the docks, wearing a scrap of faded blue around his wrist, and he was alive, and he was waiting, and she was waiting with him — and that, in all the grey, was enough to go on living for.

set.name: Viscount Marcus Wyndham
set.description: Rosalind's husband, master of Wyndham Hall; three or four grey years into the marriage his cruelty remains a schedule, not a storm, as regular as the tide. He still finds the remark that moves something behind her dead eyes (servants, runaways, the price of herring, men who work the coast) and works it slowly with satisfaction, like a splinter; he still humiliates her in company (the wrist beneath the cloth, the piano trick) and is frustrated by her flat dead-eyed calm, which he reads as a small continuing disobedience to be worked out of her. He receives hard-weathered coast men who report cargo, prices, and the state of the roads; their idle talk carried the rumour of a thin scarred dockworker with a faded blue ribbon, which the Viscount has not connected to Callum. Location: Wyndham Hall, above the sea. Goal: break her will through patient, methodical lessons and own her completely.

set.name: The Dowager Lady Wyndham (the Viscount's mother)
set.description: The Viscount's mother, grown greyer and thinner across the grey years, her pale eyes sunk deeper into her skull; she still studies Rosalind from corners, landings, and the morning-room window with needlework that is never finished, still introduces her to no one in company, still intercepts and burns Rosalind's letters (the letter to Elsie burned long ago with the household accounts; Rosalind never knew). She has not relented with the years. Location: Wyndham Hall. Goal: maintain the house's silence and order; keep Rosalind isolated and quiet.

set.name: Rosalind Wyndham (née Ashworth)
set.description: Lady Wyndham, married to Viscount Marcus Wyndham, in her early twenties; three or four grey years have passed at Wyndham Hall above the grey sea and she has stopped counting them by number. Locked each night in her high cold room with barred windows over the sea (key turned at night, morning, before dinner), she measures her life by that small bright sound and by the tide. In the third or fourth grey year she overheard — from behind the landing curtain, while one of the Viscount's hard-weathered coast men spoke in the yard — a rumour of a thin, scarred fellow working the docks at a distant port across the water who talks to no one, works like a man with nothing left to lose, and wears a scrap of faded blue tied around his wrist under his sleeve. She does not know the town's name and cannot confirm it is Callum, but she has decided it is him and refuses to be argued with by arithmetic or the grey water; the rumour is her spar, her coin, the thing she clings to like a drowning woman. The Viscount's cruelty continues as a schedule, not a storm: herring, runaways, and men who work the coast still find the crack in her calm and he works it like a splinter with satisfaction; she hides the bleeding better now, denies him her pain, and counts it a victory though she bleeds. The Dowager still studies her from corners with never-finished needlework, grown greyer and thinner. Survival has become her silent rebellion — she lets them think her broken, and underneath the dead eyes and careful smile keeps the boy, the vow, and the love alive. She still writes letters to Callum at night on the backs of bills and music leaves and burns them at the grate, sending the smoke over the sea; she keeps the sea glass sewn in the hem of her oldest gown, writes his name on the window glass in her breath, and rehearses him stitch by stitch so the pattern cannot be lost. She does not know if he lives or dies; she has decided he lives, somewhere across the water. Location: locked high room, Wyndham Hall, above the grey sea. Goal: endure the grey years, deny the Viscount her pain, keep Callum and the vow alive underneath, wait for word of him.

In the third or fourth grey year, Rosalind overheard from behind the landing curtain, while one of the Viscount's hard-weathered coast men spoke in the yard of cargo, prices, and roads, a rumour of a thin, scarred fellow working the docks at a distant port across the water who talks to no one, works like a man with nothing left to lose, and wears a scrap of faded blue tied around his wrist under his sleeve. She does not know the town's name and cannot confirm the man is Callum, but she has decided it is him and clings to the scrap of hope like a drowning woman, keeping it as her secret coin. This is the first rumour; it seeds the more detailed report of Ch. 16 placing Callum in a small coastal village far across the sea.

In Ch. 16 the more detailed rumour must give Callum's coastal village a name and reach Rosalind through some conduit (a servant's talk, a visiting merchant, a letter's fragment), so that in Ch. 18 an oilskin package can arrive at Wyndham Hall sent by that village's priest with the blue ribbon and the note of Callum's death (Ch. 18-19).

chapters.name: The Rumor
chapters.content:
The grey years kept their schedule. The key turned in the lock at night and morning and before dinner; the tide went out and came in and went out again; the herring boats crossed the strip of water below the barred window, and Rosalind gave them names and watched them become specks. And in her chest she carried the first rumour like a coin she was afraid to spend — a thin scarred man at a port on the far side of the water, a back like a map of welts, a scrap of faded blue tied around his wrist. She had decided it was him, and she would not be argued with. But there was one thing the rumour had never given her, and she felt its absence like a missing tooth: the name of the place. She could picture him; she could not reach him. The grey water kept its own arithmetic, and it would not give up its sums.

Then, one night in a season she did not trouble to name, the Viscount went away.

It happened rarely, and the house did not know how to behave. Wyndham Hall was built around its master the way a shell is built around its creature; when he left, the shell rang hollow. A ship's cargo had gone wrong at the port — a seized hold, a disputed price, money that could not wait — and Marcus Wyndham had gone down the avenue in the black carriage with his coat turned up and two of his men, leaving the house to the Dowager, which was, Rosalind thought, rather like leaving the winter to the frost. She stood at her barred window and watched the carriage go, and told herself it changed nothing. The key would still turn. The tide would still come in.

But the house, without him, loosened. It was a small loosening, almost imperceptible, the way ice loosens from a stone in the first thaw: a footman whistled in the passage and no one called him down for it; the cook's voice rose in the kitchen, arguing about fish; the maids walked the corridors as if they owned their own feet. Rosalind moved through it like a ghost, careful not to startle the brief liveliness.

And in the kitchen, where the Dowager's eye did not reach, there was a new girl.

Her name was Meg. She had come up from a farm in the spring, pink-faced and quick to smile, with round red hands and a way of looking at the tall ceilings as if they might fall on her. She had not yet learned the house's first law — that a lady is not spoken to, and a lady does not speak — and so when she brought up the evening tray herself and would have gone, Rosalind, who had taught herself never to begin speech, heard herself say, before she could stop it:

"What do they say of the weather, down at the kitchen?"

Meg turned, surprised and pleased. The lady of the house had spoken to her. That was worth a story, or several.

"They say there's a blow coming, my lady." She set the tray straight with a proprietary little pat. "My man works the packet across to the far shore, and he says you can smell it in the water a day off. He says there's queer folk over there too, in that village."

Rosalind's heart moved — a thing that had learned, over the grey years, to lie very still — and she made herself ask gently, as if it were nothing:

"Which village is that?"

"Kilbreck," said Meg, pleased to be asked. "Little place, over the water. Not a dozen houses and a church. My man's cousin fishes out of it." She leaned in, gossip gathering speed. "Says there's a fellow there came off a herring boat years back with nothing but a few pennies in oilcloth, half-starved, and the priest took him in and found him work mending nets for the fleet. Keeps to himself, talks to no one, works like a man with nothing left to lose." She dropped her voice to a whisper. "And they say his back is all scars, like a map, and he wears a scrap of blue tied round his wrist, under his sleeve, and never takes it off. Not for anything. The priest says he's waiting for someone."

Rosalind did not move. She had made her face a wall in the grey years, and she made it a wall now, and behind the wall her heart beat like a thing drowning. Herring boat, she thought. Pennies in oilcloth. The words clicked together like the pins of a lock she had thought rusted shut, and something gave, deep in her chest, with a sound only she could hear.

"Waiting for someone," she repeated, and her voice came out even, the voice she used at dinner across the candles. "That is a strange story for a kitchen, Meg."

"My man says it's true," said Meg stoutly. "Everyone in Kilbreck knows him. They call him the silent one. Never a word out of him but the prayers — the priest says he's never once missed a Sunday, sitting in the back with his head down — and afterwards he goes down to the strand and stands looking at the water." She laughed, a little embarrassed. "I told my man that's daft, standing and looking at water. But he says the fellow does it every day, like he's expecting a boat that never comes."

There was a long silence. Meg, suddenly aware of it, flushed to the roots of her hair and curtsied, and was halfway to the door when Rosalind's voice stopped her, gentler now, careful:

"Meg." The girl turned. "The Dowager dislikes gossip. You would not want her to hear that you had been telling stories to the lady of the house. I am grateful for the company. But say nothing of it, not to anyone, and I will say nothing either. It can be our small secret."

Meg's eyes went wide and bright, and she nodded hard, thrilled to have a secret with the lady, and went out, and the door closed, and Rosalind sat down on the edge of the bed with her hands folded in her lap and let the room come back to her.

Kilbreck.

She said it to the locked room, to the barred window, to the grey sea, and the word was like a key turning in a lock she had thought rusted shut. Kilbreck. Across the water. A dozen houses and a church. A fellow who came off a herring boat with pennies in oilcloth — the same boat, the same pennies, she was sure of it, she would not be argued with. A priest who took him in. A back like a map of scars — she remembered the thirty strokes, the torchlight, the shirt coming away in the yard. A scrap of blue tied round his wrist that he never took off, not for anything.

She had not known where across the water. Now she knew. Knowing it was like having a door in the grey wall — a door she could not walk through, a door no one else could see, but a door, and she pressed her hand to it in the dark the way she had once pressed her hand to the carriage glass.

That night she did not write her letter to the grate. The news was too large for ash; she was afraid that if she burned it, it would burn with it. Instead she sat at the window with the sea glass in her palm and gave herself the whole of it, piece by piece, like a woman counting coins she would never be able to spend.

She thought of his hands.

That was what the rumour had given her, really — not his face, not his voice, but his hands, because she could picture them holding the ribbon. She remembered the afternoon in the hayloft, the lantern burning low, when he had drawn the faded blue ribbon from her hair. She remembered the way he had turned it in his fingers, the blue against his brown palm, his thumb smoothing the silk as if it were something precious, as if it were her. She remembered closing his fingers around it and telling him she had never stopped loving him for one hour, and the way he had kissed it, folded it, and tucked it inside his shirt against his heart, promising to keep it till he died and after.

And now the gossip said he wore it on his wrist, where he could see it, and never took it off, not for anything.

She pictured his hands now — the hands that had mended a bridle by lantern light, that had held her face when she broke, that had saddled the two horses on the night of the ball and stood waiting in the fog — and she pictured them holding that scrap of faded blue in the dark of a hut above the strand, turning it over the way she turned the sea glass now, keeping the knowing the way he had promised. She wondered if he still kept it. She wondered if he still dreamed of her. She had decided, long ago, that he was alive, and she would not be argued with; now she decided the rest of it the same way, by refusing to let the grey water have it: he kept it, and he dreamed of her, and every day he stood on the strand looking at the water, waiting for a boat that never came.

The priest says he's waiting for someone.

Oh, but it was impossible. She knew it was impossible, the way she knew the key would turn in the lock before dawn. She was Lady Wyndham, locked each night in a high cold room with bars over the sea, watched by a Dowager whose needlework was never finished, married to a man whose pale eyes worked her like a splinter. She could not walk down to a strand on the far side of the water. The grey years had taught her arithmetic, and the arithmetic said the distance between this room and Kilbreck was the distance of an entire life, and no boat that ever crossed the sea could carry her across it.

But she let herself imagine it anyway. That was the one freedom they had never been able to take from her, and she took it now, in the dark, the way a prisoner takes air through a crack in the wall. She imagined the hut above the strand, the smell of salt and tarred net, the wind off the water. She imagined walking up the path in a plain dress — no silk, no pearls, no ring — and him turning from the door, and the way he would say her name, low, as if it cost him something, the way he had said it the first time in the hayloft. She imagined his scarred hands on her face, and the ribbon still on his wrist, the last colour she had seen before the fog closed over the long road. She imagined a life — small, grey, poor, theirs — him mending nets while she sat in the doorway with the sea in front of them, neither of them counting the years, because they would be together and the years would not matter.

She knew it was impossible. But knowing a thing was impossible had never once stopped her from deciding it was true, and she decided it now, fiercely, in the dark, with the sea glass warm in her palm: he was alive, and he was in Kilbreck, and he kept the ribbon, and he dreamed of her, and he was waiting.

And because it was impossible, she would guard it more carefully than she had ever guarded anything. The first rumour she had carried like a single coin in her pocket. This — the name, the village, the priest, the strand — was a whole purse, and the house had eyes, and one of the eyes was the Dowager's, pale and sunk and never still. She had seen the Dowager study her across the breakfast table that very morning, a beat too long, and she had smoothed her face into the mask the years had taught her and given nothing away. She would give nothing away now. She would let them think her as broken as ever, as grey as the sea; and underneath, where no hand could reach, she would carry Kilbreck like a lit lantern in her chest, the way he had carried the blue ribbon into exile.

In the morning the black carriage came back up the avenue, and the house drew itself in: the whistling stopped, the cook's voice fell, the maids became shadows again. Rosalind stood at her barred window and watched the Viscount cross the yard with his coat turned up, and her face was a wall, and behind the wall the only living thing the house had not been able to kill waited quietly, holding a name.

She said it once more to the grey sea, to the locked room, to the small bright ghost of a future she would never have:

Kilbreck.

Somewhere across the water he was standing on the strand, looking at the sea, with a scrap of faded blue around his wrist — waiting for a boat that never came, dreaming of her, keeping the knowing the way he had promised, till he died and after. And she was waiting with him, holding the name of the place where he lived like a lit lantern in the dark, refusing to let the grey water have it, refusing to be argued with, refusing, in all that grey, to stop imagining the impossible.

set.name: Viscount Marcus Wyndham
set.description: Rosalind's husband, master of Wyndham Hall; three or four grey years into the marriage his cruelty remains a schedule, not a storm, as regular as the tide. He briefly left Wyndham Hall by black carriage on a port dispute (a seized hold, a disputed price, money that could not wait) with two of his men, and while he was gone the house briefly loosened — a footman whistled, the cook's voice rose, the maids walked as if they owned their own feet — which is when the new maid Meg told Rosalind the detailed Kilbreck rumour; he has now returned up the avenue and the house has drawn itself in again. He still finds the remark that moves something behind her dead eyes (servants, runaways, the price of herring, men who work the coast) and works it slowly with satisfaction; he still humiliates her in company and is frustrated by her flat dead-eyed calm, which he reads as a small continuing disobedience to be worked out of her. He does not know of the Kilbreck rumour or of Meg's talk, and has never connected any coast talk to Callum. Location: Wyndham Hall, above the sea. Goal: break her will through patient, methodical lessons and own her completely.

set.name: The Dowager Lady Wyndham (the Viscount's mother)
set.description: The Viscount's mother, grown greyer and thinner across the grey years, her pale eyes sunk deeper into her skull; she still studies Rosalind from corners, landings, and the morning-room window with needlework that is never finished, still introduces her to no one in company, still intercepts and burns Rosalind's letters (the letter to Elsie burned long ago with the household accounts; Rosalind never knew). She studied Rosalind a beat too long across the breakfast table on the morning after the Kilbreck rumour reached her, and Rosalind smoothed her face into the mask and gave nothing away; the Dowager does not know of the rumour or of Meg's talk. She has not relented with the years. Location: Wyndham Hall. Goal: maintain the house's silence and order; keep Rosalind isolated and quiet.

set.name: Rosalind Wyndham (née Ashworth)
set.description: Lady Wyndham, married to Viscount Marcus Wyndham, in her early twenties; three or four grey years at Wyndham Hall above the grey sea and she has stopped counting them by number. Locked each night in her high cold room with barred windows over the sea (key turned at night, morning, before dinner), she measures her life by that small bright sound and by the tide. After the earlier grey-years rumour of a thin scarred dockworker with a faded blue ribbon, a more detailed rumour has now reached her in this chapter: while the Viscount was briefly away on a port dispute, the new kitchen maid Meg (from a farm; her man works the packet across the far shore) brought up the evening tray and told her the village has a name — Kilbreck, a little place of a dozen houses and a church across the water. The fellow there came off a herring boat years back with a few pennies in oilcloth, half-starved; the priest took him in and found him work mending nets; he keeps to himself, talks to no one, works like a man with nothing left to lose; his back is all scars like a map; he wears a scrap of faded blue tied round his wrist under his sleeve and never takes it off, not for anything; the priest says he is waiting for someone; he never misses a Sunday and afterwards stands on the strand looking at the water every day, like expecting a boat that never comes. Rosalind made Meg swear secrecy (and promised her own, fearing the Dowager's eyes, which studied her a beat too long that same morning) and has taken the name Kilbreck into her chest like a lit lantern. She now imagines a future again — impossible, she knows — of walking up the path to a hut above the strand, of him saying her name low as if it cost him something, of his scarred hands and the ribbon still on his wrist, of a small poor grey life together where the years would not matter; she pictures his hands holding the faded blue ribbon he took from her hair in the hayloft and wonders if he still keeps it, still dreams of her, and decides by refusal that he does. That night she did not burn a letter — the news was too large for ash — and held the sea glass instead. She will guard the name more carefully than anything, letting them think her broken while she carries Kilbreck underneath. Location: locked high room, Wyndham Hall, above the grey sea.
